title: 40 OHA 202 — IN RE GRASSHOPPER SUPPRESSION
text:
GRASSHOPPER SUPPRESSION ON LANDS ADMINISTERED BY
THE BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT IN WYOMING
DIR-2010-0046 Decided May 14, 2010
Request to the Interior Board of Land Appeals (docketed as IBLA-2010-128)
that decisions of the Bureau of Land Management be put into full force and effect.
Jurisdiction of IBLA-2010-128 assumed by the Director, Office of Hearings and
Appeals; request to put decisions into full force and effect granted.
1. Administrative Review: Generally—Rules of Practice: Appeals:
Jurisdiction—Rules of Practice: Full Force and Effect
The Director or an Appeals Board has jurisdiction to grant or
deny a request under 43 C.F.R. § 4.21(a)(1) to put a bureau
decision into full force and effect, whether or not an appeal from
the decision has been filed.
2. Public Lands: Generally
Where the Bureau of Land Management demonstrates that
immediate implementation of its grasshopper suppression
program on public lands in Wyoming is needed to avert serious
environmental and economic harm, its decisions authorizing
aerial and ground spraying of pesticides will be put into full
force and effect.
APPEARANCE: Danielle DiMauro, Esq., Office of the Regional Solicitor, Denver,
Colorado, for the Bureau of Land Management.
OPINION BY DIRECTOR ROBERT S. MORE
On May 6, 2010, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) filed with the
Interior Board of Land Appeals (IBLA) a request that decisions of ten BLM Field
Offices in Wyoming be put into full force and effect immediately, pursuant to
43 C.F.R. § 4.21(a)(1). Those ten decisions approved the use of insect growth
40 OHA 202

DIR-2010-0046
regulator and other pesticides, subject to mitigation measures, for the control of
grasshoppers on public lands.1
No party has filed an appeal to IBLA from BLM’s decisions. In In re Putah
Creek Resort Concession Agreement, 17 OHA 104 (1999), Office of Hearings and
Appeals (OHA) Director Robert Baum held that neither he nor an Ad Hoc Board of
Appeals appointed under 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(4) had jurisdiction to put a bureau
decision into full force and effect, since no appeal of the decision had been filed.
Director Baum’s holding in that case would apply equally to BLM’s request in this
case, such that IBLA would have no jurisdiction to grant the request. I have therefore
assumed jurisdiction of BLM’s request under 43 C.F.R. § 4.5(b) to consider the issue
in light of the Putah Creek Resort decision.
For the reasons explained below, I conclude that Putah Creek Resort was
wrongly decided on this point and should be overruled in part. I further conclude
that the public interest requires that BLM’s request be granted.
A. The Director or an Appeals Board has jurisdiction to put a bureau decision
into full force and effect, whether or not an appeal from the decision has
been filed.
According to § 4.21(a)(1), “A decision will not be effective during the time in
which a person adversely affected may file a notice of appeal; when the public
interest requires, however, the Director or an Appeals Board may provide that a
decision, or any part of a decision, shall be in full force and effective immediately.”
In Putah Creek Resort, the Bureau of Reclamation (BOR) filed a motion “to put
its proposed decision to terminate the Putah Creek concession agreement . . . into full
force and effect on the date that decision is issued.” 17 OHA at 107. Director Baum
denied BOR’s motion on two grounds:
First, pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 4.21, the Director can only order that a
decision be put into full force and effect (“the Director or an Appeals
1 The ten BLM decisions are April 30, and May 3, 2010, Decision Records and
Findings of No Significant Impact issued by the Buffalo, Casper, Cody, Kemmerer,
Lander, Newcastle, Pinedale, Rawlins, Rock Springs, and Worland Field Offices.
They were all based on an April 30, 2010, Environmental Assessment (EA), WY-030-
EA10- 239, which was prepared pursuant to section 102(2)(C) of the National
Environmental Policy Act of 1969, 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C) (2006). In its request and
EA, BLM uses the term “grasshoppers” to refer both to grasshoppers and Mormon
crickets.
40 OHA 203

DIR-2010-0046
Board may provide that a decision, or any part of a decision, shall be in
full force and effective immediately”) (emphasis added). Since BOR
has not issued a decision, its motion to put its future decision into full
force and effect is not ripe. Second, pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(4),
the Director’s office of OHA only has jurisdiction to review matters in
which an appeal is pending (“Appeals . . . may be considered and ruled
upon by the Director or by Ad Hoc Boards of Appeals appointed by the
Director”). Since no appeal has been filed in this case, this office does
not have jurisdiction to entertain BOR’s motion.
17 OHA at 106 (emphasis in original). I agree with the first of these holdings, but
not the second.
Director Baum correctly noted that § 4.1(b)(4) deals with appeals. It provides,
Appeals to the head of the Department which do not lie within the
appellate review jurisdiction of an established Appeals Board and which
are not specifically excepted in the general delegation of authority to
the Director may be considered and ruled upon by the Director or by Ad
Hoc Boards of Appeals appointed by the Director to consider the
particular appeals and to issue decisions thereon, deciding finally for
the Department all questions of fact and law necessary for the complete
adjudication of the issues.
Likewise, § 4.1(b)(3) deals with appellate review by IBLA (“The Board decides finally
for the Department appeals to the head of the Department from decisions rendered
by Departmental officials . . .”).
But OHA’s jurisdiction is not limited to deciding appeals. According to § 4.1,
The Office of Hearings and Appeals, headed by a Director, is an
authorized representative of the Secretary for the purpose of hearing,
considering and determining, as fully and finally as might the Secretary,
matters within the jurisdiction of the Department involving hearings,
and appeals and other review functions of the Secretary.
(Emphasis added.)
[1] As quoted above, § 4.21(a)(1) authorizes the Director or an Appeals Board
to put a bureau decision into full force and effect, including during the period
allowed for filing a notice of appeal. That period would logically include the time
before anyone actually files a notice of appeal. A bureau request that its decision be
40 OHA 204

DIR-2010-0046
put into full force and effect, if submitted before any notice of appeal has been filed,
would qualify as a “matter within the jurisdiction of the Department involving . . .
other review functions of the Secretary” under § 4.1. Thus, the Director or an
Appeals Board would have jurisdiction to grant or deny the request, even if no appeal
has been filed.
Under Director Baum’s interpretation of the regulations, if a bureau needs to
implement a decision immediately—as BLM asserts is true in this case—it may
nevertheless have to wait to submit a request under § 4.21(a)(1) until the entire
period for filing an appeal has elapsed, if no one files an appeal before the deadline.
At that point, of course, the bureau decision would take effect anyway. Thus, the
full-force-and-effect provision in § 4.21(a)(1) would be useful only in cases where a
party filed a notice of appeal significantly in advance of the appeal deadline. It is
unlikely that the Secretary intended the provision to have so limited a scope.
In fact, in several prior cases, the Secretary has directed IBLA by memorandum
to put bureau decisions into full force and effect under § 4.21(a)(1), even where no
appeal was pending.2
I conclude, therefore, that the OHA Director or an Appeals Board has
jurisdiction to consider a request that a bureau decision be put into full force and
effect under § 4.21(a)(1), whether or not an appeal of the decision has been filed.
Director Baum’s decision in In re Putah Creek Resort Concession Agreement, 17 OHA
104 (1999), is overruled to the extent it holds otherwise.
B. The public interest requires that BLM’s decisions to implement a
grasshopper suppression program on public lands in Wyoming be put into
full force and effect.
According to BLM’s May 6 request,
The enclosed decisions reflect the BLM’s determination that emergency
grasshopper and Mormon cricket suppression activities are needed on
BLM lands in Wyoming. As explained in the Background section of the
enclosed Environmental Assessment (“EA”), recent survey information
indicates that in 2010, populations of these species are likely to exceed
the “economic threshold” (“ET”) level at which the cost of damage
2 E.g., Friends of the Bow, IBLA 94-373, 94-395 (Apr. 29, 1994); In re BLM Animal
Damage Control Decision for the District of Casper, Wyoming, IBLA 94-000 (Apr. 1,
1994); In re BLM Animal Damage Control Decisions in Rock Springs and Rawlins,
Wyoming, IBLA 94-000 (Mar. 16, 1994).
40 OHA 205

DIR-2010-0046
caused by the infestation exceeds the cost of treatment. The BLM
estimates that 6.7 percent (1.2 million acres) of the approximately
18 million acres of BLM-administered lands in Wyoming are currently
threatened at an ET level by the predicted infestation of grasshoppers
and Mormon crickets.
As further detailed in the EA, grasshoppers in high densities can
severely reduce the forage value and ecological conditions of rangeland.
Grasshopper feeding causes direct damage to plants’ growth and seed
production, thus reducing valuable forage for wildlife and livestock.
Other indirect effects of severe grasshopper infestations include soil
erosion and degradation, disruption of nutrient cycles, increased risk of
weedy plant invasion or proliferation, interference with water
infiltration, and potential changes in the flora and fauna of the
rangeland ecosystem.
Request at 1-2. The request goes on to describe the serious economic harm that
could result if the threatened infestation occurs, including impacts on private
rangeland and cropland adjacent to the public lands.
BLM further notes,
Grasshopper suppression programs are most effective when
implemented in May and June, when the earliest grasshoppers hatch.
During those months, insect growth regulator pesticides may be used to
disrupt the growth of immature grasshoppers. Growth regulator
pesticides are ecologically safer and more economical than pesticides
that target adult grasshoppers.
Request at 1.
Based on these representations and the supporting material, I conclude that
the public interest requires that BLM’s decisions be put into full force and effect
immediately.
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Director, Office of
Hearings and Appeals, by the Secretary of the Interior, 43 C.F.R. § 4.1, BLM’s request
is granted, and the April 30 and May 3, 2010, decisions of the Wyoming BLM Field
Offices approving the use of pesticides for the control of grasshoppers on public lands
40 OHA 206

DIR-2010-0046
are in full force and effect. The decisions will remain in full force and effect until
IBLA takes final action on any petition for a stay or appeal that may be filed.
____________________________________
Robert S. More
Director

title: 39 OHA 259 — IN RE LAVADIE
text:
IN THE MATTER OF ELAINE B. LAVADIE
DIR-2009-0027 Decided October 28, 2009
Appeal from a determination made by a Board of Survey, New Mexico State
Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe, New Mexico, finding
employee, Elaine B. Lavadie, financially liable for damages caused by her negligence
in operating a U.S. Government-owned vehicle, a 2005 Ford Explorer 4x4, vehicle
number I-421898, Report of Survey No. GDRS090001.
Reversed.
1. Property Board of Survey: Negligence: Motor Vehicle
A Report of Survey determination of employee liability in simple
negligence will be reversed when the record reflects that the
motor vehicle accident at issue was not the result of the
employee’s failure to exercise the degree of care that a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances.
2. Property Board of Survey: Administrative Procedure: Generally:
Employee Participation
A determination of employee liability in simple negligence
will be reversed where the employee was not given an
opportunity to provide a written statement and make an
oral presentation to the Board of Survey prior to its
determination of findings.
APPEARANCES: Elaine B. Lavadie, Santa Fe, New Mexico, pro se.
39 OHA 259

DIR-2009-0027
OPINION BY CHAIRMAN BRUCE A. JOHNSON
Introduction
Elaine B. Lavadie (Appellant), an employee with the New Mexico State Office,
BLM, Santa Fe, New Mexico, has appealed the January 28, 2009, decision of the
Reviewing Official, affirming the findings and determinations of the Board of Survey
(Board), New Mexico State Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe,
New Mexico, finding her negligent and financially liable for damage to Government-
owned property, a 2005 Ford Explorer 4x4 truck, vehicle number I-421898, arising
out of a October 5, 2007, accident at the U.S. Post Office in Santa Fe, New Mexico.
Pursuant to 410 DM 114-60.808-4, Appellant was assessed $250 in damages. The
decision was transmitted to Appellant by memorandum dated January 29, 2009,
from Gwen Rush, Property Utilization Specialist, National Business Center, BLM,
Denver, Colorado. Appellant’s appeal was received by the Office of Hearings and
Appeals on March 2, 2009, and was assigned Docket No. DIR-2009-0027. BLM
transmitted the official file to this Office on March 16, 2009. The file consists in
pertinent part of: the Report of Survey (GDRS090001), signed by the Reviewing
Official on January 28, 2009, with the attached report of the Board; an estimate for
repair from CF Collision, Santa Fe, New Mexico, in the amount of $410.29; an
estimate for repair from Crystal Clear Body Shop, Inc., Santa Fe, New Mexico, in the
amount of $369.81; and an estimate for repair from Mobile Auto Restoration Service,
Espanola, New Mexico, in the amount of $264.45. There were no photographs of the
damaged vehicle in the file.
Apparently, Appellant did not file an official accident report form, Standard
Form 91; however, in describing the accident in an “Accident Report”, she stated
that:
I drove a Government vehicle (Ford Explorer, New Mexico license
number 1421898) to the U.S. Post Office [2010 S. Pacheco, Santa Fe, NM] to
drop off the outgoing mail for the Bureau of Land Management. I dropped the
mail off at the loading dock. I had my seat belt buckled and my mirrors
adjusted; I proceeded to back-up out of the dock area. I did not back out far
enough prior to turning in order to swing out and drive forward, therefore I
bumped into a short (about 4 feet high) concrete pole (which I did not see in
the mirror or through the back window). I sustained small property damage
to the passenger side of the bumper. I came back to the office and verbally
reported the incident to Darlene Ortiz, Property Manager Specialist. I was also
going to report it to Charles Byrd, Regional Safety Officer, but he was out of
the office.
Accident Report, dated October 5, 2007.
39 OHA 260

DIR-2009-0027
There is no indication in the record that the Chairperson, Board of Survey,
New Mexico State Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Santa Fe, New
Mexico, notified Appellant that a Board of Survey was being initiated to determine
employee liability concerning her accident or that Appellant was informed of her
right to submit a written explanation of the circumstances surrounding the accident
and to make an oral presentation to the Board. There is a memorandum dated
January 16, 2009, in the file from the Board Chairperson to Appellant providing her
with the Board’s Findings and Recommendation.
The Board of Survey Decision
In its findings and determination dated January 16, 2009, the Board found
Appellant liable for “simple negligence” in the amount of $250.
In explaining its finding, the Board stated:
The Board has found the employee accountable for simple
negligence. Based on further discussion with the employee, the Board
feels if the employee would have utilized the driver/passenger side
mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles on both sides of the vehicle
and not cut her turn too short.
Board of Survey Findings, dated January 16, 2009.
By memorandum dated January 29, 2009, Gwen Rush, Property Utilization
Specialist, National Business Center, BLM, Denver, Colorado, informed Appellant that
she had been found negligent and financially liable for damage to the vehicle
resulting from her October 5, 2007, accident.
Argument on Appeal
In her appeal, received on March 2, 2009, Appellant indicates that she wishes
to contest the determination of the Board of Survey. First, Appellant argues that she
had not been given proper training in the operation of this size vehicle, stating that:
I am appealing a determination of simple negligence for the damage of
Government vehicle number 1421898. I am requesting relief from
accountability in the amount of $250....
A more fair solution would have been for the Survey Board to
recommend proper training on the operation of large Government Vehicles.
39 OHA 261

DIR-2009-0027
I have always driven small cars; this vehicle is a large Ford Explorer 4x4. I
have never had any training driving a large vehicle.
. . . .
The only reason I was driving a large vehicle was because the mail
courier service that had a contract to pickup and deliver the mail for the New
Mexico State Office closed overnight. They did not notify us (or their
employees) that they were closing. The Bureau of Land Management decided
not to pay a professional mail courier to continue courier service. The
responsibility of getting the mail to and from the post office was passed on to
the two employees sharing the duties of the mail clerk position (I was one of
them). My supervisor, at the time, suggested to me that I use my personal,
new, vehicle to run back and forth to the post office. Because the person I
shared the mail duty with took the bus to work, he would have to use my car.
I did not want the vehicle’s interior being scuffed up with the mail bins, etc.
and more important, I did not want someone else driving my car. It was then
decided that a Government Vehicle would be dedicated to us for the sole
purpose of picking up the morning mail and taking the outgoing mail in the
afternoon.
With respect to the convening of the Board of Survey, the fact that she did not
receive notice and her knowledge of the Board proceedings, Appellant stated that:
I do not think that policy (if there is a policy) regarding notification
that an employee is to appear before a Board was followed. I was not given
written notice that I was going to be called before the board. The accident
happened on October 5, 2007. It was 15 months before I was called,
without prior notice, to appear before the Board. After the Board met
regarding my case, I found out that other employees receive a memorandum
notifying them of the meeting and instructing them on what to do and when
to be there. The day I was called before the Board, I was attending
Correspondence Training - someone who knew where the training was
being held came and called me out of training to appear before the board. I
did not know I was going to testify. This was my only experience before such
a board - in fact I did not know exactly what a Board of Survey does - I do
now.
Next, Appellant provides her perspective on the findings of the Board
regarding her negligence stating that:
39 OHA 262

DIR-2009-0027
The accident happened in the afternoon when I was backing up out of
the loading dock at the U.S. Post Office; I had dropped off the outgoing mail.
My written statement said I used my mirrors, yet I was asked if I used my
mirrors, I stated that I did (but I still did not see the object I backed into - it
could have been in a blind spot). Now, upon reflection, I wonder if I was
being tricked into incriminating myself. I know that I did all the things I
should have done prior to backing up - I did not see anything in my path. No
one witnessed the accident, but I immediately reported the incident. That
should demonstrate integrity.
I was assured by the person I reported the accident to that the damage
was so minor and the vehicle was going to be excessed soon, so I should not
be overly worried. I was asked to submit a written explanation, enter the
accident online into the Safety Management Information System, and take the
vehicle for estimates. I did the first two but was never able to take time from
my duties to take the vehicle to any shops for estimates.
At the time of the accident, I had multiple duties which included:
• Staff Assistance for the Branch of Support Services;
• Quicktime lead for New Mexico/Oklahoma/Texas/Kansas; and
• Mail clerk (a temporary duty which started in April 2007). This later
became a shared position until August 18, 2008 when the other person
quit and it again became my duty.
All those positions have tight deadlines and I was never able to leave
the office to take the vehicle for estimates. During that time period, I was
many times assured not to worry about the estimates because the damage was
so small.
In December 2008 when a full time mail person was hired, the Bureau
of Land Management also hired a professional courier service; I was finally
able to take time to take the vehicle for estimates.
Appeal, dated February 26, 2009.
Review of the Survey Decision
[1] At issue in this case is whether the Board of Survey properly concluded
that the damage to the Government vehicle resulted from simple negligence on the
39 OHA 263

DIR-2009-0027
part of Appellant. Simple negligence, as defined at 410 DM 114-60.808-1(b)(2), is
“an act or omission of the employee where they failed to exercise the degree of care,
precaution, attention, and vigilance that a prudent person would exercise under like
circumstances.” Where an employee exercises the degree of care which a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances, the fact that an accident occurs will
not render the employee liable. 410 DM 114-60.808-1(a).
It has been recognized in the general law of employee liability that an
employee has a duty to his employer to exercise a reasonable degree of care, skill,
and judgment in the performance of his duties of employment. 27 Am. Jur. 2d
Employment Relationship § 220 (1996); 30 C. J. S. Employer-Employee Relationship
§ 111 (1992). With regard to the relationship between operation of Government
vehicles and the influence of outside factors on that operation, some guidance is
provided by principles of negligence law. Courts have held that an individual’s
conduct is a legal cause of the event if it was a material element and a substantial
factor in bringing it about. 57A Am. Jur. 2d Negligence § 435 (1996). To be a
material element and a substantial factor in a negligent act, there must be some duty
violated.
The record in this case does not support the determination of simple
negligence. In its findings, the Board based its determination of simple negligence on
the conclusion that “if the employee would have utilized the driver/passenger side
mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles on both sides of the vehicle and not cut
her turn too short.” The Board’s conclusion is in direct conflict with Appellant’s
October 5, 2007, written statement which she made at the time of the accident. In
her statement, Appellant indicated that:
I dropped the mail off at the loading dock. I had my seat belt buckled
and my mirrors adjusted; I proceeded to back-up out of the dock area. I did
not back out far enough prior to turning in order to swing out and drive
forward, therefore I bumped into a short (about 4 feet high) concrete pole
(which I did not see in the mirror or through the back window).
In her appeal, Appellant states that when asked by the Board, she informed the
Board that she had used the mirrors when backing up in the vehicle, but did not see
the pole which may have been in a blind spot. Appellant states that she had also
noted this in her October 5, 2007, written statement which was made at the time of
the accident. Despite two statements by Appellant that she used the mirrors, the
Board concluded without explanation that if she had “utilized the driver/passenger
side mirrors, she would have seen the 4 ft. poles [sic] on both sides of the vehicle.”
The Board made no effort to explain its conclusion, which is not in accord with
Appellant’s statement of the facts. Despite Appellant’s statement that she did not see
the concrete pole, the Board did not indicate how it resolved this conflict. The Board
does not state that it found Appellant’s statement unbelievable, nor did the Board go
39 OHA 264

DIR-2009-0027
to the scene to view the pole and the surroundings to determine if Appellant’s version
was feasible or correct. There are no photographs of the scene, which may have
helped either to support the Board’s conclusion or Appellant’s version of the accident.
At a minimum, where there is a direct conflict between the Board’s conclusion and
Appellant’s statement of what happened, the Board should attempt to resolve the
conflict by explaining its reasoning or indicate that it does not accept Appellant’s
version, either because it is not believable or it is not supported by other evidence.
In view of the preceding, we conclude that Appellant’s version of the accident
is credible and there is nothing in the file to contradict her statement that she did not
see the pole when looking in the mirror or through the rear window. In this case, the
Board clearly did not prove negligence by Appellant in her operation of the
Government vehicle.
Therefore, we conclude that Appellant’s conduct did not constitute simple
negligence, and she is not financially liable for $250.
[2] With respect to the notice that the Board of Survey must give an employee,
the Departmental Manual provides in pertinent part that:
(a) Prior to convening a board of survey the Chairperson, Board of
Survey or Survey Officer will send written notification to the employee
who may be held liable for property loss, and afford the employee the
opportunity to present a written statement of facts surrounding the loss.
Any such statement must be presented to the Board of Survey/Survey
Officer by the employee within fourteen (14) calendar days of the date
of the notification. The statement(s) will become part of the Report of
Survey and will be considered in the investigation and determination of
financial liability.
(b) The employee may also orally address the Board within the same
time frame, but must provide an accompanying written statement of
any facts they wish the Board to include in the Report of Survey.
410 DM 114-60.808-2.
In this case, there is no evidence that Appellant was notified that she had the
opportunity to address the Board through a written statement and make an oral
presentation as provided in the Departmental Manual. In fact, Appellant states in her
appeal that she did not receive notice from the Board.
The Departmental Manual does not provide specific instructions for notifying
employees of the opportunity to present written and oral statements on their behalf.
The Departmental Manual only states that “written notification” will be sent to the
39 OHA 265

DIR-2009-0027
employee and that the employee will be afforded the opportunity to present a written
and an oral statement of the facts surrounding the property loss. 410 DM 114-
60.808-2. This lack of notice is troubling because had she been afforded the
opportunity to prepare for the Board meeting and to address the issues prior to a
decision, Appellant may have persuaded the Board, in accordance with 410 DM
§ 114-60.808-1(a), not to hold her liable, and thus obviated the need for any further
proceedings. We have held that where due process is not afforded and the employee
is not provided a fair opportunity to present evidence for the Board of Survey’s
consideration in determining its findings, the Board of Survey’s determination of
simple negligence on the part of the employee will not be affirmed on appeal. See In
re Susan LaFranchi-Madonich, 24 OHA 73 (2003); In re Don E. Skaggs, 12 OHA 106
(1996); In re David B. Luttrell, 13 OHA 176 (1996). The Board in this case did not
ensure that the Appellant was notified in accordance with the Departmental Manual.
While a lack of diligence on the part of the cognizant employee or
obstructionist tactics may justify the Board’s going forward in his/her absence, that is
not the case here. Glaring procedural inconsistencies and a lack of explanation in the
record, such as was found in this case, undermines the integrity of the Board of
Survey process and warrants reversal of the Board’s decision. See In re Loretta Park,
17 OHA 116 (1999); In re William M. Wilson, 13 OHA 156, 161 (1996); In re
Judith M. Kish, 13 OHA 185, 187-89 (1996).
The evidence shows that the Board in this case made no effort to provide the
employee with a fair review of her case before determining that she was negligent
and financially liable. The Board did not convene until 15 months after the accident,
yet there is no explanation why there was such a lengthy delay. After the 15-month
delay, the Board did not send Appellant the requisite notice that the Board would
review her case and that she could provide a written statement and appear in person
before the Board. Instead of providing the requisite notice of her opportunity to
appear, the Board orally summoned Appellant to its meeting. Without notice,
Appellant was called from a training session to appear before the Board. Without an
opportunity to prepare her points and a presentation, Appellant appeared before the
Board and according to her, she “testified”. Appellant does not indicate what she
“testified” to, nor does the Board provide an indication of the content of her
“testimony”. It is unclear why the Board thought this was appropriate, or complied
with the DM provisions regarding the review to be performed by a Board of Survey.
The fact that the Board called the employee before the Board on the day it met does
not satisfy the DM requirements. To expect the employee to leave a training session
and, without notice, appear before an investigatory body, such as the Board, is
patently unfair and contrary to Departmental requirements, and basic fairness.
Based upon the preceding, we conclude that the Board failed to provide
Appellant with the minimum notice required by the DM and did not permit her to
make a written presentation to the Board as required by the DM. Moreover, we
39 OHA 266

DIR-2009-0027
conclude that the personal appearance before the Board provided by the Board was
not in accordance with the DM requirement. Accordingly, we reverse the Board’s
decision finding Appellant negligent and financially liable for $250.
We find, therefore, that Appellant was not negligent in her operation of the
Government vehicle and that she is not liable, pursuant to 410 DM 114-60.808-4 (a),
for $250.
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 43 C.F.R § 4.1(b)(4); 410 DM 114-60.808-7.
____________________________________
Bruce A. Johnson
Chairman, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
I concur:
____________________________________
James L. Byrnes
Member, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals

title: 43 OHA 236 — IN RE SHUGERT
text:
IN THE MATTER OF MATTHEW SHUGERT
DIR-2011-0073 Decided September 20, 2011
Appeal from an Administrative Wage Garnishment Notice issued by the U.S.
Department of the Treasury at the request of the National Operations Center, Bureau
of Land Management, U.S. Department of the Interior, finding former employee,
Matthew Shugert, financially liable for a debt in the amount of $1,408.29, Federal
Debt Case ID Number 2008084040A.
Affirmed, the debt to the United States is valid.
1. Administrative Wage Garnishment: Burden of Proof
In an administrative wage garnishment proceeding, the relevant
regulation, 31 C.F.R. §285.11(f)(8), requires that the agency has the
burden of going forward to prove the existence of the debt.
Thereafter, the debtor must establish by a preponderance of the

the Evidence

evidence to rebut the agency case concerning the existence of

Review of the Debt Validity
[1] In an administrative wage garnishment proceeding, the relevant regulation,
31 C.F.R. §285.11(f)(8), requires that the agency has the burden of going forward to
prove the existence of the debt. Thereafter, the debtor must establish by a
preponderance of the evidence that no debt exists or that the amount of the debt is
incorrect.
BLM has submitted a Receipt for Property signed by the Appellant on
September 2, 2004. Among the items listed are “Nokia G250 cell phone
707/498-7252” and “Property Number - 0429252 Bendix King Hand Held Radio,
GPH Model # 5102x Quantity 1 S/N 022008.” Also contained in the BLM record are
U.S. Cellular cell phone bills to BLM for the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, dated July 18, 2004, September 18, 2004, October 18, 2004,
November 18, 2004, and December 18, 2004.
The foregoing items, along with the statements by Appellant’s former BLM
Supervisor regarding Appellant’s failure to return these items, were contained in the
record reviewed and relied upon by the California BLM Board of Survey in
determining the liability of the Appellant for the amount of the administrative wage
garnishment. After reviewing BLM’s record, I have determined that these
submissions, taken as a whole, are sufficient to meet BLM’s burden of establishing the
debt as valid. The record establishes that the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, and the Bendix King Hand Held Radio were assigned to Appellant
and that he acknowledged such. The statements of Appellant’s Supervisor and the
decision of the Board of Survey also substantiate BLM’s allegation that Appellant
43 OHA 241

DIR-2011-0073
failed to return said items and continued to use the Nokia G250 cell phone, number
707/498-7252, for his personal use, including a period after he vacated his BLM
position. Therefore, the burden of proof in this proceeding shifts to the Appellant to
show, by a preponderance of evidence, that the debt is not valid.
[2] Appellant attempts a collateral attack on the decision of the California BLM
Board of Survey process, asserting variously that he was not informed of the
proceedings and that his Supervisor submitted “falsified and forged documentation”
to the Board, which caused the Board to issue an incorrect decision.
As evidence of being excluded from the proceedings, the Appellant has
submitted a copy of an envelope sent to his address, which was returned with the
notation “Return to Sender [-] Shugert, Matthew Moved Left No Address [-] Unable
To Forward [-] Return To Sender.” However, the address in question was the
Appellant’s address of record which he had on file with BLM. This Office has
consistently ruled that a person will be deemed to have received the communication
if it was delivered to his last address of record in the appropriate office of the Bureau
of Land Management, regardless of whether it was in fact received by him. See, e.g.,
Joel Carothers, 179 IBLA 244, 248-250 (2010); Arthur M. Solander, 79 IBLA 70, 73
(1984). BLM has issued a wide variety of letters, bills, and demand letters to the
Appellant in an attempt to resolve this debt. The fact that Appellant discontinued the
use of the address he had on file with BLM and failed to either submit a change of
address to BLM or file a forwarding request with the Postal Service is a defect of his
own making.
As noted above, the Board’s decision in this matter was issued in 2005.
Appellant’s collateral attack on its conclusion at this late date must fail since the
decision is considered settled under the doctrine of administrative finality. In re San
Tan Irrigation District, 30 OHA 1, 13-14 (2005). The doctrine of administrative
finality, the administrative counterpart of the doctrine of res judicata, dictates that
once a party has had an opportunity to obtain administrative review of an agency
decision within the Department and the decision has been upheld on appeal, the
decision may not be reconsidered in subsequent proceedings, except upon a showing
of compelling legal or equitable reasons. Gifford H. Allen, 131 IBLA 195, 202 (1994).
However, a precondition for the application of the principle of res judicata is that the
matter raised in the subsequent proceeding was one distinctly put in issue and
directly determined in the earlier litigation. State of Alaska, 140 IBLA 205, 211
(1997). The precise issue before the Board was Appellant’s liability for the debt in
question. Thus, BLM is entitled to rely on the Board’s decision in this matter in
making a determination of liability.
[3] Further, I have completed a review de novo of all the evidence submitted by
BLM and the Appellant and conclude that the Appellant has failed in his effort to
43 OHA 242

DIR-2011-0073
show the debt is not valid. Appellant makes numerous allegations of “falsified and
forged documents” and allegedly false statements made by his former BLM
Supervisor. However, the bulk of his allegations and accusations involve the issue of
the termination of his employment with California BLM. These issues are irrelevant
to this hearing, since the only issue I decide is the validity of the debt caused by the
failure to return the Nokia G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252, and the Bendix
King Hand Held Radio upon the termination of his employment with BLM.
After a thorough review of Appellant’s submissions, I conclude that they are
neither credible nor persuasive. Appellant contends that his employee copy of the
September 2, 2004, DI-105 Receipt for Property, shows that the Bendix King Hand
Held Radio was never assigned to him. I disagree. The DI-105 clearly shows
19 items charged to Appellant’s care for use in his job. The radio is listed as Item 17
and its property number is clearly stated. Since the DI-105 was handwritten and
contains only items that were assigned, it is impossible to conclude that the radio was
not assigned to Appellant. While Appellant is correct that there were further
handwritten interlineations made to this entry on his former Supervisor’s copy,
possibly sometime after he signed it, they appear to have been made to clarify which
particular radio was missing. The Appellant’s signature is identical on both copies of
the DI-105. Therefore, the essential element of proof that the Bendix King Hand Held
Radio was actually assigned to him must be decided in favor of BLM. I note that
other than a general denial, Appellant has made no attempt to explain why this one
item on a DI-105, containing 18 other items, would be singled out as missing or how
this matter was handled during the check-out process.
As to the other portion of the debt in question, the Appellant was notably silent
regarding the disposition of Nokia G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252. This
item is also clearly listed on the DI-105, demonstrating Appellant’s acknowledgment
that it was assigned to him for BLM job related use. The U.S. Cellular phone bill for
this phone, dated July 18, 2004, shows the total charges amounted to $28.13. The
charges for the bill dated September 18, 2004, show an amount due of $26.17.
However, the charges for the bill dated October 18, 2004, show a total amount
due of $554.73. A review of the individually billed phone calls reveals that,
consistent with BLM’s claims, these phone calls were placed from a variety of
locations throughout the western states and to a wide variety of phone numbers in
various states. This pattern is repeated on the bill dated November 18, 2004, with a
total amount due of $755.39. The same is true of the bill dated December 18, 2004,
with a due amount of $117.42.
Of particular note, one of the many addresses contained in the case file for
Appellant is an address in Mount Pleasant, Michigan. Appellant discloses in his filing
that this is his family’s address. Among the numerous phone calls made on the Nokia
43 OHA 243

DIR-2011-0073
G250 cell phone, number 707/498-7252, none of which seem to have any relevance
to his employment with BLM, are phone calls made to Mount Pleasant, Michigan.
Some of the calls were placed to cell phone numbers in Mount Pleasant. However,
there is a series of calls spread over the phones bills to 989/773-1533, a land line
phone number in Mount Pleasant, Michigan. I hereby take administrative notice that
a check of the internet White Pages phone book reveals that this number is related to
the Appellant in this matter. It therefore is unlikely that these calls were made by
anyone other than the Appellant. I conclude that BLM has established the validity of
the debt in the matter and that Appellant has failed to show he does not owe the
amount in question. Appellant is required to pay the amount requested by the U.S.
Department of the Treasury.
Based on the foregoing, I rule that the debt to the United States is valid. The
U.S. Department of the Treasury is requested to proceed with the administrative
wage garnishment.
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 31 C.F.R. § 285.11(f)(12).

ORDER
By petition dated October 31, 2001, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) has
requested that the Director, Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA), assume jurisdiction of these
cases pursuant to 43 CFR 4.5(b) and review the October 24, 2001, order of the Interior Board of
Land Appeals (IBLA) granting a stay of BLM’s September 7, 2001, final grazing decisions
issued to the appellant-permittees.1/ BLM argues that IBLA committed “clear legal error” in
granting the stay sought by appellants (Petition at 11) and that the stay “causes great harm to
BLM’s ability to take measures required under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and a court-
approved settlement to protect the endangered [sic] desert tortoise” (Id. at 1-2).2/
1/ The County of San Bernardino, California, is also an appellant in these cases and had
likewise sought a stay of BLM’s September 7 decisions.
2/ The Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has listed the Mojave population of the desert
tortoise as a threatened, not an endangered, species. 55 FR 12178 (1990). See Blincoe v. Bureau
of Land Management, No. CA-690-01-01 (OHA Hearings Division, Aug. 24, 2001) (hereinafter
“ALJ Decision”) at 7. The distinction is not significant for purposes of this litigation.
20 OHA 63A

D 2002-5
By notice and order dated November 3, 2001, I denied BLM’s petition as to most of the
appellant-permittees and gave the parties until November 13, 2001, to submit any additional
arguments, supporting declarations, and/or documents they might have on the issue of whether I
should assume jurisdiction of the cases involving the remaining appellant-permittees. Responses
were received from BLM and from appellants Richard Blincoe and Dave Fisher. For the reasons
set forth below, I hereby grant BLM’s petition in part and vacate IBLA’s October 24 stay
decision in part.
Facts and Procedural Background3/
In March 2000, the Center for Biological Diversity and other plaintiffs (the Center) filed
suit against BLM, alleging that BLM had failed to consult with FWS regarding the cumulative
effects on federally listed species of all actions authorized by BLM’s California Desert
Conservation Area (CDCA) Plan, in violation of § 7(a)(2) of the ESA,16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2).
Center for Biological Diversity v. Bureau of Land Management, No. C 00-00927 WHA (N.D.
Cal.). The Center further alleged that BLM was violating the ESA by allowing those activities,
including livestock grazing, to continue in the absence of consultation with FWS, citing Pacific
Rivers v. Thomas, 30 F.3d 1050 (9th Cir. 1994). As relief, the Center sought an injunction
against all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan and an order directing BLM to initiate and
complete consultation on the programmatic effects of the CDCA Plan on all federally listed
species.
The Department of Justice (DOJ), in consultation with BLM, decided to negotiate a
settlement of the case because BLM had not, in fact, consulted with FWS at the land use plan
level regarding the cumulative effects of all the activities authorized by the CDCA Plan but,
rather, had only engaged in a series of programmatic-level consultations regarding the isolated
effects of selected activities. It appeared likely to DOJ and BLM, in light of the Pacific Rivers
case, that if the matter were litigated, all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan would be
enjoined for BLM’s failure to consult on the cumulative effects of all authorized activities.
Eventually, the Center and BLM executed a total of five court-approved stipulations requiring
BLM to take various actions regarding a wide range of activities authorized under the CDCA
Plan in order to protect the desert tortoise and other listed species.
Stipulation 3, approved by the court on January 29, 2001, addressed livestock grazing
activities in desert tortoise habitat. Among other things, it provided for the seasonal exclusion of
cattle from a portion of the public lands identified as desert tortoise habitat within each of 11
grazing allotments, including appellants’, from March 1 to June 15 and from September 7 to
3/ This summary of the facts and procedural background of the case is taken largely from
the August 24 ALJ Decision at 6-19 and the October 24 IBLA Stay Decision at 1-3.
20 OHA 63B

D 2002-5
November 7 each year. Stipulation 3 specified the acreage of desert tortoise habitat to be
included in each exclusion area but not the precise location.
On April 9, 2001, BLM issued an Environmental Assessment (EA), evaluating a proposal
to temporarily modify existing livestock grazing permits in accordance with Stipulation 3.
Significantly, the EA contained an evaluation of 42 allotments to determine whether conditions
warranted emergency action pursuant to 43 CFR 4110.3-3(b). The EA concluded
that conditions, while serious, do not constitute an emergency at this time. Continued
grazing does not pose an “imminent likelihood of significant resource damage” to soils,
wildlife habitat, vegetation, and other critical values in the 42 allotments. The BLM has
been actively involved in modification of grazing practices since 1991 that has led to
improved conditions for the desert tortoise and its habitat over many [of] these
allotments. The proposed action would be an additional step to alleviate resource damage
from continued livestock grazing.
EA at 87.
On May 15, 2001, BLM issued a decision record approving the proposed action of the
EA. On the same day, BLM issued final grazing decisions to the appellant-permittees and others,
modifying the terms of their grazing permits. The final grazing decisions excluded cattle from
identified areas of desert tortoise habitat on each of 11 allotments during the spring and fall
exclusion periods; reduced the annual amount of permitted cattle use for several of the
allotments, capping it at the average number of animal unit months (AUMs) actually used for the
1997, 1998, and 1999 billing years; and imposed other restrictions to protect certain riparian
habitat areas.
Consistent with Stipulation 3, the final grazing decisions provided that
[i]f during the periods of exclusion cattle are found in the exclusion areas you will
have 48 hours after notification to remove them. If they are not removed within 48 hours,
trespass action according to 43 CFR § 4150.2(a), (b) will be taken and an additional day
will be added onto the exclusion period for every day they remain in trespass.
September 7 Decisions at 5.
BLM explained in both the decision record and final grazing decisions that it had agreed
to a settlement in the Center for Biological Diversity lawsuit “[i]n order to comply with the ESA,
as well as to preclude the potential for a desert wide injunction” against the “wide and varied”
uses of desert land authorized in the CDCA Plan. Decision Record at 5.
20 OHA 63C

D 2002-5
These interim agreements allowed BLM to continue appropriate levels of activity
throughout the planning area during the lengthy consultation process while providing
protection to the desert tortoise and other listed species in the short term. By taking
interim actions as allowed under 43 CFR Part 4100, BLM contributes to the conservation
of the endangered and threatened species in accordance with [§] 7(a)(1) of the ESA.
BLM also avoids making any irreversible or irretrievable commitment of resources which
would foreclose any reasonable and prudent alternatives which might be required as a
result of the consultation on the CDCA Plan in accordance with [§] 7(d) [of] the ESA.
* * * * * * *
The BLM’s decision is a temporary modification to current livestock grazing
administration pending completion of a Biological Opinion on the affects of the CDCA
Plan and implementation of any applicable requirements.
The BLM’s decision will provide the highest level of protection for the desert
tortoise and its habitat of any option analyzed in the EA. The cumulative impact of
reducing sheep and cattle grazing on 42 allotments will result in a slight improvement in
the existing resource conditions for the tortoise and other listed and sensitive species until
the Biological Opinion is prepared and BLM can review and implement its requirements.
Id. at 4-6.
Appellants challenged the May 15 final grazing decisions in notices of appeal filed on
June 13 and 15, 2001. By memoranda dated June 15 and 18, 2001, the Secretary assumed
jurisdiction of the appeals pursuant to 43 CFR 4.5(a) and assigned the cases to Administrative
Law Judge (ALJ) Harvey C. Sweitzer for hearing and issuance of a decision. Under a special
delegation of authority set forth in each memorandum, the Secretary provided that Judge
Sweitzer’s decisions in the cases would be final for the Department. The cases were
consolidated for a hearing, which was held in late July and early August 2001.
On August 24, 2001, Judge Sweitzer issued a 103-page decision, in which he reached the
following conclusions of law:
(1) The EA and Decision Record are legally sufficient under NEPA [the National
Environmental Policy Act];
(2) The final grazing decisions are not arbitrary and capricious, are not an abuse of
discretion, are supported upon a rational basis, and are otherwise in accordance with the
law, except as provided in conclusion (4) below;
(3) The final grazing decisions are consistent with section 7 of the ESA; and
20 OHA 63D

D 2002-5
(4) BLM complied with the grazing regulations when it issued the final grazing decisions,
except that BLM failed to comply with the requirement of consultation, cooperation, and
coordination [CCC] with the affected permittees and therefore the final grazing decisions
are hereby set aside and the matters remanded to BLM for further action consistent with
this Decision.
ALJ Decision at 103.
With respect to his fourth conclusion, Judge Sweitzer analyzed in detail the CCC
requirement as found in 43 CFR 4110.0-5 and 4.110.3-3(a), the applicable IBLA precedent, and
the extent of BLM’s communications with the appellant-permittees prior to its issuance of the
final grazing decisions. In finding that BLM had failed in its CCC obligations, Judge Sweitzer
concluded, “Consultation is an important component of an informed and rational decision
making process. Appellants should be afforded a real opportunity to contribute information and
shape the actions to be taken for the mutual benefit of all parties and the affected resources.” Id.
In response to Judge Sweitzer’s decision, BLM sent a letter to each of the appellants on
August 31, 2001, inviting them to “participate in a consultation, cooperation, and coordination
workshop regarding implementation of the court-approved Settlement Stipulations at issue in this
matter.” The workshop was scheduled for September 6-7, 2001. BLM stated that the purpose of
the workshop was to seek appellants’ “advice and exchange views on relevant issues and
proposed management actions relevant” to the final grazing decisions. BLM advised appellants
that, after fulfilling the requirements for CCC, “it is the BLM’s intent to issue revised grazing
decisions.” Appellants were asked to let BLM know, if they could not attend the workshop,
when they could meet; they were also told they could submit written advice and comment.
Similar letters were sent to the County and members of the interested public; and BLM states that
it followed up with telephone calls to the permittees, the State, and the County.
From August 28 through September 6, counsel for the respective parties engaged in
telephone conversations and exchanged correspondence over the timing and purpose of the
proposed CCC workshop. Counsel for BLM invited counsel for the permittees to submit
proposed modifications to the grazing decisions, and if any of the permittees were unable to
attend the workshop, to provide their recommendations “for adjusting the exclusion boundaries
and outlining their particular concerns so that we may discuss and address them.” After checking
with her clients, counsel for the permittees responded that “the vast majority” were unable to
meet on September 6-7, but proposed alternative meeting dates of September 13-14 or the first
week in October. Counsel for BLM responded that the meeting would take place on
September 6-7 and made reference to a “suggested conference call”; counsel further stated that
BLM intended to issue grazing decisions that would be immediately effective on September 7.
Counsel for the permittees replied that they would be unable to attend the proposed meeting on
20 OHA 63E

D 2002-5
September 6-7, but she reiterated the permittees’ offer to meet one week later and submit written
and oral comments at that time.4/
On September 5, the County responded to BLM’s August 31 invitation to the
September 6-7 CCC workshop. The County said that BLM’s letter had just arrived the day
before and that “it is impossible for the County to provide its input on such short notice * * *.”
The County assured BLM that it wanted to participate in the consultation process and requested
that the workshop be postponed to a date that would allow all the parties “an opportunity to
prepare a meaningful presentation.” Evidently the County did send two representatives to the
September 6 session with BLM, but no other interested parties appeared.
On September 7, 2001, BLM issued new, immediately effective final grazing decisions to
the appellant-permittees. The decisions recounted the procedural history of the case and cited at
length the evidence presented at the July-August hearing concerning the continuing decline of the
desert tortoise. BLM also detailed its attempts at CCC following Judge Sweitzer’s August 24

In deciding whether to grant or deny a request for a stay, a board or the Director must
consider the four factors set forth in 43 CFR 4.21(b)(1):
(i) The relative harm to the parties if the stay is granted or denied,
(ii) The likelihood of the appellant’s success on the merits,
(iii) The likelihood of immediate and irreparable harm if the stay is not granted, and
(iv) Whether the public interest favors granting the stay[.]
Under § 4.21(b)(2), an appellant requesting a stay has the burden of proof that a stay should be
granted. As explained in the 1993 preamble to § 4.21, “the burden is on the appellant to

As noted above, Judge Sweitzer’s August 24 decision documents the multiple threats to
the desert tortoise posed by grazing operations, as well as the “near total collapse of tortoise
populations in the Mojave.” ALJ Decision at 29. “The recent severe and catastrophic declines in
desert tortoise populations in California signal a need for new and immediate action to reduce all
sources of mortality and to stabilize populations.” Id. at 24. Moreover, as Judge Sweitzer noted,
Congress in the ESA has afforded listed species “‘the highest of priorities.’ TVA v. Hill,
437 U.S. 153, 174 (1978). Under the ESA, the balance of the hardships has already been struck
in favor of endangered species * * *.” Id. at 76. Indeed, “under the ESA, federally listed species
are to be * * * protected, whatever the cost. [TVA], 437 U.S. at 174, 184.” Id. at 96-97
(emphasis in original).
20 OHA 63R

D 2002-5
Of course, like Judge Sweitzer’s statements about economic harm cited previously, these
conclusions were reached in the context of a decision on the merits, not a stay request. It would
certainly be possible to argue that, over the limited duration of a stay, any harm to the desert
tortoise would be much less severe, particularly if the stay included the months between seasonal
exclusion periods. But appellants’ stay requests and motion to IBLA for expedited review sought
to avoid the entire fall 2001 exclusion period, and there is no guarantee that a decision on the
merits of the appeals will be rendered by the start of the spring 2002 exclusion period. Given the
already dire and worsening condition of desert tortoise populations in the Mojave, a stay that
would permit grazing during even one exclusion period would run counter to the public interest
as expressed by Congress in the ESA.
In addition, granting a stay preventing implementation of Stipulation 3 in the Center for
Biological Diversity suit would pose significant risks for BLM and potentially all activities
authorized in the CDCA Plan. Judge Sweitzer described BLM’s decision to negotiate a
settlement of that litigation as follows:
BLM personnel thought the threat of injunction was high, especially for activities
in critical habitat * * *, which is reasonable in light of the § 7(a)(2) mandate to insure that
activities do not adversely modify critical habitat. In sum, BLM reasonably assumed that
an injunction of all activities authorized under the CDCA Plan was likely if it litigated the
Federal court action, and its efforts to reach compromise under such circumstances should
not be discouraged based upon the evidence presented.
ALJ Decision at 65.
In addition to harming the desert tortoise, therefore, a stay in this case could lead the
Center to seek to reopen the litigation in order to prohibit all activities authorized by the CDCA
Plan, pending completion of the lengthy consultation process with FWS. Such a prohibition, of
course, would have far-reaching consequences for BLM, appellant-permittees, the County, and
all users of the CDCA. I therefore find that both the relative harm to the parties and the public
interest militate against granting the stay.
Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Director by 43 CFR
4.5(b), I hereby grant BLM’s petition with respect to appellants Fisher and Mitchell and vacate
IBLA’s October 24, 2001, stay decision with respect to those appellants. All appeals from
20 OHA 63S

D 2002-5
BLM’s September 7, 2001, final grazing decisions will be forwarded to the Hearings Division for
a hearing and decision on the merits.

April 9, 2004
IN THE MATTER OF : Docket No. D 2003-49
RALPH L. MAIZE :
: Waiver Request and Appeal
:
: Waiver Request Granted in Part;
: Waiver Appeal Denied
ORDER
On March 28, 2003, the Supervisor, Taxes and Collections Group, Payroll
Operations Division (POD), National Business Center, Office of the Secretary, Denver,
Colorado, filed with the Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) an appeal from
Ralph L. Maize, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), from its
denial of his request for a waiver of salary overpayments in the amount of $2,658.91,
Bill for Collection 13330018911. In an Amended Administrative Report, dated
March 24, 2003, POD indicated that “There were two adjustments made to
Mr. Maize’s payroll records in November 2001, each resulting in a bill for collection
(No. 13190018911, $3,047.90 and No. 13330018911, $2,490.38 [this debt figure
increased to $2,658.91 after adding $168.53 for year-end taxes]).” In a second
Amended Administrative Report, dated December 1, 2003, the total overpayment was
indicated to be $11,812.95. As stated below, POD recommended granting waiver of
$9,154.05 and denying waiver of $2,658.91. In those documents, POD filed a
request on behalf of Mr. Maize for waiver in the amount of $9,154.04.
The record shows that the overpayment was discovered on July 31, 2001, and
Mr. Maize was informed of the overpayment on that date. POD prepared an
Administrative Report, dated June 28, 2002, which accompanied Mr. Maize’s request
for waiver and explained the circumstances of the salary overpayments as follows:
Mr. Ralph Ma[i]ze, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), received erroneous overpayments when his agency did not
terminate his pay retention in a timely manner (March 17, 1997).
(Administrative Report, POD 2002-142, at 1.)
27 OHA 244

D 2003-49
In a letter to Mr. Maize dated July 31, 2001, Sherian L. Long, State Personnel
Officer, California State Office, Bureau of Land Management, stated:
It has recently come to our attention that the pay retention was not
terminated at the end of the two years, i.e. March 20, 1997. This was
due to an administrative oversight. We recognize if we were to now
process this termination of retained pay with the original effective date,
it would cause you undue financial hardship. Therefore, your retained
pay will be terminated effective July 29, 2001, and your pay will be set
at grade 9, step 10 which is $47,739 for a Law Enforcement Officer.
(Letter to Ralph Maize from Sherian L. Long, State Personnel Officer, dated July 31,
2001.)
5 U.S.C. § 5584(a)(2) provides that the head of an agency may waive claims
against employees arising from erroneous overpayments of pay when the “claim is in
an amount aggregating not more than $1,500.” 5 U.S.C. § 5584(a)(2)(A). In this
case, it appears that the Agency determined not to seek collection of the
overpayments Mr. Maize received from March 20, 1997, through July 29, 2001,
because requiring repayment would cause undue financial hardship to Mr. Maize.
The Agency’s failure to issue a bill for collection to Mr. Maize for the entire amount of
the overpayment amounts to a waiver of that amount and is not authorized. Waiver
authority with respect to current employees can only be exercised by POD and the
Office of Hearings and Appeals. Waiver authority with respect to former employees
may be exercised by the Bureau and the Office of Hearings and Appeals. A bill for
collection must be issued for the overpayment before a waiver can be granted. See
344 DM 9. Moreover, financial hardship cannot be the basis for a waiver. On
July 21, 2003, this Office contacted Dora Meyer, POD, regarding this matter.
Ms. Meyer indicated that she would look into the matter and contact the Agency.
Ms. Meyer subsequently informed this Office that BLM would be conducting a new
audit of Mr. Maize’s pay, a new bill for collection would be issued, and POD would
submit a second amended Administrative Report. On December 8, 2003, the second
Amended Administrative Report was received from POD indicating the total amount
owed by Mr. Maize as $11,812.95 (Bills for Collection: M0332100001, $6,106.14;
13190018911, $3,047.90; and 13330018911, $2,658.91).
The December 1, 2003, Amended Administrative Report prepared by POD
explained the circumstances of the salary overpayment as follows:
Mr. Ralph Ma[i]ze, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), received erroneous overpayments of salary when his pay
retention status was not terminated in a timely manner. Employee was
27 OHA 245

D 2003-49
entitled to pay retention until March 17, 1997, at which time he should
have received 50 percent of the annual comparability increase paid to
general schedule employees.
Mr. Maize received a letter from his State Personnel Office dated
July 31, 2001, stating: “By letter dated December 2, 1994, you were
notified of management’s decision to move your position, Criminal
Investigator, GS-1811-11, from Ukiah to Barstow, California. You were
also informed that you would be given a directed reassignment to this
new duty location. In lieu of this reassignment, management gave you
the option of accepting a position change in a vacant Law Enforcement
Ranger, GS-1801-9, located in your current geographical area of Ukiah.
The letter stipulated that if you selected this option, you would be given
pay retention for two years. By memorandum dated January 17, 1995,
you accepted the GS-9 position.”
(Amended Administrative Report, POD 2002-142, at 1.)
The December 1, 2003, Amended Administrative Report also indicated the following:
The Division of Payroll Operations stated that there were two
adjustments made to Mr. Maize’s payroll records in November 2001,
each resulting in a bill for collection (No. 13190018911, $3,047.90 and
No. 13330018911, $2,490.38). These bills initially appeared to be
duplicated, however, the adjustments reflected different corrections to
the employee’s pay. Debt No. 13190018911, is the difference between
the full annual increase, and 50 percent of the annual increase, which is
what the employee was entitled to under Pay Retention. Debt ID
13330018911 represents the pay reduction due to pay retention being
terminated, effective July 29, 2001.
An additional bill for collection, was generated in November 2003,
which represents the overpayments for the period prior to the above-
billed amounts (March 1997 through October 2000).
(Amended Administrative Report, POD 2002-142, at 2.)
In the December 1, 2003, Amended Administrative Report, POD made the
following recommendations with respect to Mr. Maize’s request for waiver:
We find that the circumstances of this case are that Mr. Maize was
initially unaware that he was receiving erroneous overpayments of
27 OHA 246

D 2003-49
salary. Mr. Maize was advised that upon acceptance of the GS-09
position, that he would be entitled to retained pay for two years.
Therefore, as of March 1997, Mr. Maize should have only received 50
percent of the cost of living adjustments. However, there is nothing in
the record, which indicates that the employee was advised regarding
the specifics of his retained pay status and the effects on his annual
increases. Mr. Maize could not reasonably be expected to know or
understand the complexities of the Federal personnel regulations and
payroll procedures implementing and canceling grade retention and the
impact of those actions on cost of living and step increases.
Accordingly, we conclude that Mr. Maize was not at fault in this matter
up to the official notification by his office on July 31, 2001, that an
error had occurred. Therefore, we recommend approval of his waiver
request in the amount of $9,154.04 (OHA Decision D 99-59[)].
However, Mr. Maize did receive a written notification on July 31, 2001,
that he was being paid in error and corrections to his salary would be
made. The letter advised him that if he had any questions, to contact
his personnel staffing specialist. He was aware upon receipt of his leave
and earnings statements, that in fact, his pay had not been reduced and
that he was receiving pay beyond his entitlement. This is substantiated
in Mr. Maize’s letters of February 10, 2002 and July 15, 2002, w[h]ere
he stated that he knew he was not receiving the correct rate and
detailed his hourly rate. We appreciate the fact that employee inquired
as to the accuracy of his pay, and that administrative delays occurred,
however, when an employee has knowledge of an overpayment of pay
but does not set aside funds in anticipation of refunding it to the United
States, then employee is guilty of “Lack of Good Faith” and waiver is
precluded by law (CG Decision No. B-183558), therefore, we
recommend denial [of] Mr. Maize’s request for waiver in the amount of
$2,658.91.
(Amended Administrative Report, POD 2002-142, at 2-3.)
In light of the information included in the December 1, 2003, Amended
Administrative Report, on January 23, 2004, Teresa M. LeBlanc, Chair, Ad Hoc Board
of Appeals, sent a memorandum to Mr. Maize requesting additional information.
Mr. Maize was asked to provide an additional statement in response to the amended
report; specifically, Mr. Maize was asked to address his knowledge of the Agency’s
offer of grade or pay retention.
27 OHA 247

D 2003-49
In a February 10, 2004, memorandum, Mr. Maize provided an additional
statement to this Office. Mr. Maize indicated that his SF-50's (Notifications of
Personnel Action) show that his pay grade was a GS 9, Step 10. Mr. Maize indicated
that he received several bills that were for different amounts and that payroll began
deducting $200.00 from his pay even though his waiver appeal was not final. In
response to the request for information regarding his knowledge of pay or grade
retention, Mr. Maize stated:
I hope your office is in receipt of all the responses I have submitted
regarding this matter. One thing that is troubling is in regards to the
information you have requested, that being, my knowledge of the
Agency’s offer of grade retention and/or pay retention. This
information is the basis for the current action. This information was
previously submitted, but I did include it again, per your request.
(Memorandum to OHA from Ralph L. Maize, dated February 10, 2004.)
OHA exercises the Secretary of the Interior's delegated authority to waive
collection of erroneous payments over $1,500 from employees of the Department of
the Interior and its constituent bureaus. POD has authority to waive debts of less
than $1,500 arising out of erroneous payments under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). If
POD denies a waiver request, an appeal can be made to this office.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA is authorized to waive claims for
overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity and good conscience
and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority may not be exercised
if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good faith by the
employee or any other person having an interest in obtaining a waiver of the claim.
See 344 DM 9 (1998). Waiver determinations under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 are based
solely on the facts and circumstances giving rise to the erroneous payment and the
employee’s knowledge or fault in the matter. See e.g., In re Fred M. Ritchhart,
18 OHA 47, 49 (1999). In the instant case, it is undisputed that the erroneous
overpayments made to Mr. Maize occurred as the result of an administrative error.
It is well settled by decisions of the Comptroller General that where an
employee was aware or should have been aware of an overpayment of pay when it
occurred, the employee cannot reasonably expect to retain such payments, but should
set them aside and expect the Government to seek recovery. Additionally, the
employee should make provision for repayment of the overpayments. Gilbert G.
Quintero, B-183558, April 23, 1975; Bruce C. Hanson, B-260849, Sept. 19, 1995. In
these circumstances, the employee is not entitled to relief under 5 U.S.C. § 5584. In
such cases, collection of an overpayment is not considered to be against equity, good
27 OHA 248

D 2003-49
conscience, or contrary to the best interests of the United States. See Joan R.
Edwards, B-271616, Oct. 3, 1996; Sandra L. Geer, B-243686, July 2, 1991;
L. Mitchell Dick, B-192283, Nov. 15, 1978.
Waiver is not proper if the employee was aware that he had received an
overpayment. Amadeo Martinez, Jr., B-261628, June 13, 1996. Decisions of the
Comptroller General state that where an agency notifies an employee of an
overpayment, the employee is on notice and precluded from relying on the accuracy
of the overpayment. In such cases, waiver is not appropriate since collection of the
overpayment by the agency would not be against equity and good conscience despite
the absence of fault on the part of the employee. John Wessels, B-265874, May 22,
1996.
The issue in this case is whether Mr. Maize can be said to have acted in good
faith in this matter. The Comptroller General has consistently held that requests for
waiver will be denied when the employee requesting the waiver was aware of the
overpayment when it occurred. Gilbert G. Quintero, supra. In that case, an
employee’s failure to set aside overpayments of which he was aware was found to be
a lack of good faith. In this case, while Mr. Maize had no reason initially to be aware
of the overpayments, he was notified on July 31, 2001, of the overpayments and,
once notified, should have made provision for repayment. The standard employed by
the Comptroller General and OHA is to determine whether a reasonable person
should have been aware that he was receiving a payment to which he was not
entitled. The circumstances in this case are that Mr. Maize was placed on grade
retention and then pay retention following his decision to remain in Ukiah, California
after his GS-11 position was reassigned to Barstow, California. Mr. Maize’s pay was
not computed correctly once he was on retained pay status and he continued to
receive his full cost of living increases instead of 50 percent of the increases as
provided for in the pay regulations. The Agency discovered the error and notified
Mr. Maize on July 31, 2001, that his pay would be corrected to reflect the correct
amount. Due to a subsequent administrative error, Mr. Maize’s pay was not corrected
until the SF-50 (Notification of Personnel Action) was processed on November 5,
2001.
We agree with POD that the record does not indicate that Mr. Maize was
counseled as to the effects of grade and pay retention on his pay. It may be that the
agency should consider instituting a policy of providing such information in writing
to employees. We find that Mr. Maize was unaware of the overpayments initially and
should not be required to repay the overpayments that occurred prior to his
notification on July 31, 2001. After that date, Mr. Maize was aware that he was
receiving pay to which he was not entitled and therefore is not entitled to a waiver
for the remainder of the overpayments in the amount of $2,658.91. See Steven P.
Bell, B-228661, Aug, 18, 1988.
27 OHA 249

D 2003-49
In summary, on the basis of the record before us, we find that Mr. Maize’s lack
of good faith in this matter precludes a waiver. We find that it would not be against
equity and good conscience and the best interests of the United States to deny his
request for waiver in the total amount of $2,658.91, Bill for Collection 13330018911.
Accordingly, his waiver appeal is denied. Mr. Maize is entitled to waiver of the
remainder of the overpayment, $9,154.04, Bills for Collection M0332100001 and
13190018911, as stated above. In accordance with the above, Mr. Maize’s waiver
request is granted in part in the total amount of $9,154.04.
Pursuant to 344 DM 9 (1998), this decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter.

OPINION BY CHAIRMAN JAMES L. BYRNES
Pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 7.37, Pensco Trust Company, Appellant, filed on
February 10, 2014, in this Office a Notice of Appeal and a Request for a Stay of the
decision issued by Administrative Law Judge Robert G. Holt on January 9, 2014, in
Pensco Trust Company v. BLM, ARPA 2013-01 (2014). Judge Holt found in his
decision that Appellant violated the Archaeological Resources Protection Act of
(ARPA), 16 U.S.C. §§ 470aa-470mm (2006), and that the civil penalty of
$101,540.80, as assessed by the Field Manager, Shoshone Field Office, Bureau of
Land Management (BLM), Shoshone, Idaho, was a reasonable and appropriate
penalty for the violation. BLM alleged that Appellant erected a building and other
improvements on public land adjacent to Appellant's Dry Creek Ranch and that
during the unauthorized construction it bladed through an archaeological site on the
west side of the building. Pursuant to ARPA, BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80
47

for restoration of the site and the destruction of the archaeological resource. The
administrative record in the proceeding as well as the submissions of Appellant were
received and reviewed by this Board. By Order dated March 20, 2014, we denied the

In its Notice of Appeal, Appellant asserts that the "record does not support the
findings that agents of Pensco or independent contractors caused the alleged
damage." Appellant also asserts that the "record does not support the finding that
there was damage to and archaeological resource, the amount of the assessed value
by the BLM or who caused the damage." Appellant further contends that the
Administrative Law Judge erred when he held that deficiencies in the Notice of
Violation and Notice of Assessment did not bar BLM from assessing civil damages.
This is essentially the entirety of the Appellant's argument and presentation. Under
43 C.F.R. § 4.703, Appellant had 30 days from the date of filing its appeal to submit
briefing to support its contentions. For whatever reason it did not. Thus, we have
only vague and generalized allegations of error in the decision under appeal.
[1] To prevail in an appeal of a decision of an Administrative Law Judge,
Appellant must specify the errors alleged with particularity and support those
allegations with specific evidence. In re Jack Lee Harebon, 27 OHA 225, 228 (2004).
After an examination and careful consideration of the decision of the Administrative

sees no reason to disturb any portion of the Administrative Law Judge's ruling,

attached to this Opinion. The instant appeal is hereby denied. Judge Holt's decision
in the civil penalty proceeding of Pensco Trust Company v. BLM, ARPA 2013-01,
(2014), is affirmed and adopted.

MANAGEMENT (BLM),
