DECISION
Appearances: Philip A. Brown, Esq., Gooding, Idaho, for Complainant
Anne Corcoran Briggs, Esq., Boise, Idaho, for Respondent
Before: Administrative Law Judge Robert G. Holt
I. Introduction
This matter is before me on a request for hearing filed by Pensco Trust Co.
("Pensco") pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 7.15 (g). The Bureau of Land Management
("BLM") has assessed a civil penalty against Pensco for violation of the
Archaeological Resources Protection Act of 1979 ("ARPA"), 16 U.S.C §§ 470aa -
470mm (2006).
BLM has alleged that Pensco erected a building and other improvements on
public land adjacent to Pensco's Dry Creek Ranch and that during the unauthorized
construction it bladed through an archaeological site on the west side of the
building. BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80.
47 OHA 11

ARPA 2013-01
At the hearing, Pensco presented evidence that neither its trustee nor its
manager bladed or authorized others to blade the archaeological site. Nevertheless I
find that the evidence shows that only Pensco agents or its contractors had access to
the site and that they caused the damage to the site. Because Pensco had ultimate
control of the activities at the site, ARPA makes it responsible for the damages.
The following sections will first provide more background information, then
discuss the burden and standard of proof, and finally analyze why Pensco is liable.
II. Background
The Gooding County Planning and Zoning office first made BLM aware of a
house being built on public lands. Tr. 83:23-84:6. Further investigation showed that
a house was being constructed on BLM land lying north of property owned by
Pensco known as the Dry Creek Ranch. BLM Exs. 6, 7,and 10. The land is located
northwest of Gooding in south central Idaho. BLM concluded that Pensco was
responsible for the unauthorized construction because it held the grazing permit on
the BLM land and controlled the only vehicle access through a locked gate on its
private land. See Tr. 94:9-96:3, BLM Exs. 8 and 10.
Upon further investigation BLM concluded that the activities around the
house may have disturbed an archeological resource in violation of ARPA. As a
result, BLM sent a staff archaeologist to the site to record and assess the damage. She
prepared a June 2012 assessment which concluded that the site exhibits
numerous remains of past human life or activities which are of
archaeological in excess of 100 years old, it meets the definition of an
archaeological resource according to the Archaeological Resources Protection Act
(ARPA) as amended (16 U.S.C. 470bb(l))...." BLM Ex. 1 at 3.
She described damage to the archaeological resource caused by the blading of
a road to the west of the house construction. She calculated the total damages to be
$101,540.80. This included the archaeological value of the resource ($98,371.76) plus
the cost of restoration and repair of the site ($3,169.04). Id. at and 11.
BLM then issued Pensco a Notice of Violation ("NOV") (Pensco A),
followed by a Notice of Assessment ("NOA") declaring that Pensco was responsible
for the damage to the archaeological site caused by the unauthorized blading and
house construction. BLM reaffirmed the two components of the proposed penalty of
$101,540.80: $98,371.76 for the archaeological value of the archaeological resource
2
47 OHA 12

ARPA 2013-01
and for the cost of restoration and repair of the site. Pensco subsequently
filed a Request for Hearing regarding the NOA.
BLM filed a motion for summary judgement before the hearing. I denied the
motion because genuine fact issues remained, specifically whether Pensco was
responsible for the blading of the road to the west of the house. In the course of
denying the motion I also ruled in BLM's favor on several alleged deficiencies in
NOV and NOA. Pensco v. BLM, No. ARPA 2013-01 (Dept. of Interior,
Hearings Division, filed Sep. 3, 2013).
I conducted a one day hearing on September 24, 2013 in Shoshone, Idaho. At
the conclusion of testimony the parties declined oral argument in favor of written
submissions and then subsequently stipulated to dispensing with written post-
hearing briefs. Consequently this decision is made without the benefit of argument
from either counsel.
The following sections will address the issues I believe were raised by the
hearing.
III. Analysis
A. Burden and Standard of Proof
Neither ARPA nor its implementing regulations establish the burden and
standard of proof for hearings. But a Department of the Interior appeals board
decision has affirmed an administrative law judge decision that placed the burden
on the Government to prove both the fact of violation and the propriety of the.
penalty assessment by a preponderance of the evidence. In re Harelson, 27 OHA 225,
228 (2004) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 556(d) (2000) and of v. Greenwich Collieries,
512 U.S. 267, 276-78 Accordingly BLM must prove by a preponderance of
This description of the standard and burden of proof differs from that articulated
in two prior administrative law judge decisions. Both of these required that
the [Government] bears the burden of going forward with evidence
sufficient to establish a prima facie case as to the fact of violation and
the propriety of the penalty assessment. If a prima facie case is
presented, the burden then shifts to complainant(s) to overcome [the
Government's] prima facie case.
3
47 OHA 13

ARPA 2013-01
the evidence that Pensco is responsible for the alleged violation and that the penalty
assessment is appropriate.
The Responsibility of Pensco
BLM found that the damage to the archaeological resources had been caused
by blading with heavy equipment on the west side of the house construction site
and that Pensco was responsible. Pensco Ex. A. See Tr. 94:9 - 104:13 - 105:3,
107:19 - 108:23 (testimony of BLM realty specialist). It supported this finding with
evidence that heavy equipment had done the damage, that a person could not easily
access the site with heavy equipment over public land, and that Pensco controlled
the only access for heavy equipment through its private land to the south. Id., Tr.
94:9 - 96:3, 104:13 - 105:3, 107:19 - 108:23 (testimony of BLM realty specialist). See
BLM Exs. 6 and 10. Further Pensco's manager, Mr. Brown, and its trustee, Mr. Saiya,
acknowledged that a contractor hired by Pensco, and Pensco itself, had heavy
equipment on the construction site. Tr. 166:7-24 (Mr. Brown), 188:3—7 (Mr. Saiya).
Pensco, through the testimony of its manager and trustee, expressly denied
that it was responsible for the archaeological damage. They asserted that they had
not bladed the area and had expressly instructed all the contractors' employees not
to use the road on the west side of the house. Mr. Saiya did not want to obstruct the
view from the house and just wanted it to go back to nature. Tr. 155:2—159:1 (Mr.
Brown), Tr. 177:9-180:11 (Mr. Saiya).
I did not find that either Mr. Brown or Mr. Saiya testified credibly. Mr. Brown
testified that he did not remember the name of the excavation contractor on the site.
Tr. 166:11 Yet he remembered the number of its employees he instructed not to
use the west road. Tr. 167:24—168:12. And he remembered the specific instruction he
gave. Tr. find it incredible that he could not remember the name of the
contractor but could remember the instruction and the number of employees he
gave the instruction to. In addition Mr. Brown did not provide the details that one
would expect about such a significant instruction, i.e., when he gave it, where he
gave it, and the other circumstances of his instruction. Consequently I find it more
likely than not that he did not give the instruction at all, or at least not before the
damage occurred.
Eel River Sawmills, Inc. v. United States, Nos. ARPA 90-1 & 90-2, at 3-4 (Dept. of
Interior, Hearings Division, Aug. 10, 1992). Accord Ariz. Silica Sand Co. v. Acting Area
Dir., Bureau of Indian Affairs, No. at 9-10 (Dept of Interior, Hearings
Division, Oct.
4
47 OHA 14

ARPA 2013-01
Mr. Saiya had a better memory about the identity of the excavation
contractor. After first stating that he could not remember the name of the contractor
he identified the contractor as "Petit Construction." Tr. 178:4—18. Then he related
that the contractor started work on its own initiative, without express instructions
from Mr. Saiya, without a written contract, without an agreement on price, and
without written plans. Tr. 182:11-15, 186:4-6, 186:22-187:8. Given these
circumstances, I find it incredible that Mr. Saiya had instructed this contractor not to
use the west road. See 188:10—190:22. Mr. Saiya would have had no need to give
such a specific instruction before the contractor began work at the site because Mr.
Saiya had not even told the contractor to begin. Therefore I find it more likely than
not that Mr. Saiya did not give the instruction at all, or did not give it with the
specificity he related at the hearing. At least Mr. Saiya did not give the instruction
before he learned that the contractor had begun work, thus leaving the possibility
that the damage had already been done before the instruction.
But even if I could accept the testimony of Mr. Brown and Mr. Saiya, Pensco
would still be responsible for the damage. This conclusion requires determining
whether ARPA imposes liability on a party who did not damage the archaeological
site itself and who gave express instructions not to disturb the area where the
damage occurred.
Neither the ARPA statute nor the implementing regulations expressly impose
liability on persons who did not physically damage an archaeological resource. The
statute states:
No person may excavate, remove, damage, or otherwise alter or
deface, or attempt to excavate, remove, damage, or otherwise alter or
deface any archaeological resource located on public lands
16 U.S.C. § 470ee(a). And the content of this statutory section is reiterated in the
regulations at 43 C.F.R. § 7.4(a). But neither of these prohibitions limits liability to
only the person who physically caused the damage.
Where a statute, such as ARPA, does not expressly provide for expanded
liability nor foreclose it, the courts often apply common law principles like,
"vicarious liability," to interpret it. See Mey v. Pinnacle Security, LLC, 2012 WL
4009718 (N.D. W.Va.), at *4 (citing Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280, 285 (2003) ("[W]hen
Congress creates a tort action, it legislates against a legal background of ordinary
tort-related vicarious liability rules and consequently intends its legislation to
5
47 OHA 15

ARPA 2013-01
incorporate those rules.")); BUC Intern Corp. v. International Yacht Council Ltd., 489
F.3d 1139 (11th Cir. 2007) (Where a statute does not specifically provide for
vicarious liability, well established principles derived from common law apply.)
In a situation analogous to ARPA, the courts have held that the Federal Mine
Safety and Health Act of 1977, 30 U.S.C §§ 801-965 (2006) ("MSHA") imposes
responsibility on a mine operator for the violations of another person, even though
the statute did not explicitly provide for it. Like ARPA, MSHA, does not expressly
provide for expanded liability nor does it expressly limit liability to only the person
who physically violated the statute. Nevertheless in Western-Fuels-Utah, Inc. v.
Federal Mine Safety & Health Review 870 F.2d 711 (D.C. Cir. 1989), the court
held a mine operator responsible for the actions of its miner who negligently
violated an MSHA regulation, even though the operator had not been negligent
itself, and could not have foreseen the violation. Id. at 713, 716. The court explained
the underlying common law doctrine:
The general rule of both civil and criminal responsibility is that
a person is not liable for a harm done unless he caused it by his action
(actus reus ), and did so with a certain intent (mens rea ). Strict liability
alters this general rule by eliminating the requirement of mens rea; one
may then be punished for acting in a forbidden way, even if one was
without any particular intent, such as willfulness or negligence. A
familiar example is the strict liability of an enterprise for the
consequences of its ultrahazardous activity, such as the use of
explosives. Vicarious liability, on the other hand, alters the general rule
by holding a person liable for the act of another-that is, by attenuating
the requirement of an actus reus. A familiar example here is the liability
of one coconspirator for the act of another within the scope of the
conspiracy.
Vicarious liability may be imposed with or without regard to
the intent of the actor; in the latter case, which combines strict and
vicarious liability, one person is held liable for an act of another who
was not at fault. An innkeeper, for example, may be liable, both civilly
and criminally, for serving an alcoholic beverage to a minor even if he
has taken action to ensure that minors not be served in his
establishment, was unaware that a minor was being served, and could
not, in the exercise of reasonable care, have stopped the minor from
being served. See W. LaFave and A. Scott, Criminal Law 224-25 (1972).
6
47 OHA 16

ARPA 2013-01
Id. at 713. Prior hearing decisions have held that ARPA establishes a strict liability
standard for civil penalties. Eel River Sawmills, Inc. v. United States, Nos. ARPA 90-1
& 90-2, at (Dept. of Interior, Hearings Division, Aug. 10, Accord Ariz.
Silica Sand Co. v. Acting Area Dir., Bureau of Indian Affairs, No. at 11
(Dept. of Interior, Hearings Division, Oct. 21, 1996).
The evidence shows that either Pensco itself (by Mr. Brown or Mr. Saiya), or
its excavation contractor, must have disturbed the ground on the west side of the
building where BLM found the archaeological damage. Pensco and its contractor
had the heavy equipment capable of doing the damage on site and Pensco controlled
the only roads capable of bringing the heavy equipment to the site. No other actors
have been identified as being at the construction site. Since Mr. Brown, Mr. Saiya,
and the contractor were acting for the benefit of Pensco, it was responsible for their
actions under the doctrine of "vicarious liability."
If the statute were interpreted otherwise, it would allow a person, such as
Pensco, to escape liability for its employees or contractors simply by claiming that
they acted contrary to its instructions. Interpreting the statute to impose vicarious
liability on Pensco promotes the purpose of ARPA - to protect irreplaceable
archaeological resources on public lands. See 46 Fed. Reg. 5566 (Jan.
("[ARPA] has two fundamental purposes: to protect irreplaceable archeological [sic]
resources on public lands . . . ; and to increase communication . . . .").
In this instance the contractor was trespassing on the public lands at the behest of
Pensco and Pensco should bear the ultimate responsibility for the damage to the
archaeological resources.
Having concluded that Pensco is responsible for the damage to the
archaeological resources, attention will now turn to whether BLM properly
calculated the penalty assessment.
The Propriety of the Penalty Assessment
The Government prepared a written Damage Assessment that found a
disturbance of 1,163 cubic yards, covering 7,279 square feet, to an archaeological
resource on public land administered by BLM. It found that the unauthorized
disturbance caused damage to the resources in the total amount of $101,540.80,
consisting of repair and restoration ($3,169.04) and archaeological value ($98,371.76).
BLM Exhibit 1 at BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80 equal to the
amount of damages documented in the Damage Assessment.
7
47 OHA 17

ARPA 2013-01
At the hearing BLM introduced a map showing the approximate site
boundaries (BLM Ex. pictures of the disturbed area (BLM Ex. and a map
showing locations of disturbed archaeological artifacts such as flicks and stone tools
(BLM Ex. 7). The BLM archaeologist who prepared the Damage Assessment
testified. And testimony from an Idaho deputy state historic preservation officer (Tr.
112—129) and a Shoshone Bannock tribal cultural resources coordinator (Tr. 129—
135) supported the archaeologist's testimony.
Pensco presented no opposing evidence or argument to counter the damage
assessment evidence. Nevertheless its cross examination appeared to challenge the
archaeologist's measurement of the disturbed area. See BLM Ex. 1 at 10. Pensco
developed evidence that the archaeologist had not actually measured the depth of
the disturbed area. Tr. 38:16-40:3. Rather the witness said she had used a uniform
depth of two inches, which she described as an "educated estimate." Tr. 40:4 - 20.
Further testimony from the state historic preservation officer established that the
BLM archaeologist had "used a conservative estimate as to depth at just five
centimeters, or two inches .. ." Tr. 120:2 - 121:11. After reviewing the testimony I
find that BLM reasonably used an estimate of two inches to calculate the volume of
the disturbed area and that the use of this estimate did not diminish the propriety of
the damage assessment.
Pensco's cross-examination of the archaeologist also attempted to question
the source of the artifacts (Tr. 42:12-44:17, 51:13-52:6), whether cows could have
caused the damage (Tr. 44:18 - 46:13), whether the site met the regulatory definition
of an archaeological resource (Tr.46:14-50:11), and whether the resource had been
actually damaged (Tr. 50:12-51:12, 52:7-53:7). But, effective redirect examination
successfully rehabilitated the witness. Tr. 53:15 - did not find that the cross-
examination undermined the evidence presented by BLM.
Pensco also seems to question whether the site satisfied the required 100-year
age. See Pensco Ex. A at 1 ("exact age of the site could not be determined"). But the
archaeologist opined that that the site was older than 100 years because the artifacts
must have been left before the Shoshone Bannock and Shoshone tribes were
removed to reservation in the Tr. 28:1 — 11.
In summary I conclude that BLM proved, by a preponderance of the
evidence, that its penalty assessment (in an amount equal to the damage to the
archaeological resource) was appropriate.
8
47 OHA 18

ARPA 2013-01
IV. Conclusion
The above analysis has shown that Pensco is responsible under ARPA for the
damage done to archaeological resource on BLM land because ARPA imposes
vicarious liability upon Pensco for the actions of its employees or contractors. And
the evidence has shown that the penalty assessment is appropriate. Therefore I
conclude that BLM has proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Pensco is
responsible for the alleged violation and that the penalty assessment is appropriate.
The civil penalty assessed by BLM against Pensco for violation of the
Archaeological Resources Protection Act in the amount of $101,540.80 is affirmed.

title: 26 OHA 31 — IN RE SANDERFORD
text:
November 7, 2003
IN THE MATTER OF : Docket No. D 2003-34
JANE SANDERFORD :
: Waiver Appeal
:
: Request for Reconsideration
: Denied
ORDER
On October 9, 2003, Ms. Jane Sanderford filed a petition for reconsideration
pursuant to 344 DM 9.6C (1998) of the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals September 17,
2003, decision styled In the Matter of Jane Sanderford, 25 OHA 257 (2003). The
Board’s decision affirmed the denial by the Payroll Operations Division (POD),
National Business Center, Office of the Secretary, Denver Colorado, of
Ms. Sanderford’s request for waiver of salary overpayment in the amount of
$1,788.75 as identified in Bill for Collection No. Q2760014585. Ms. Sanderford,
an employee of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), had sought a waiver under
the provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000).
In its Administrative Report, POD 2002-285, prepared on December 5, 2002,
POD set forth the circumstances surrounding the overpayment of salary as follows:
Jane Sanderford, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), received erroneous overpayment when her award was input
with the incorrect amount. The award was to be for $2,500.00 and was
input as $5000.00.
(Administrative Report POD 2002-285, at 1).
26 OHA 31

D 2003-34
The Administrative Report included a summary of a letter from BLM in which
BLM explained that the amount to be paid to Ms. Sanderford was the topic of two
conversations between the BLM Personnel Specialist and the BLM Supervisory, Realty
Specialist. During the first conversation, the Personnel Specialist informed the
Supervisory, Realty Specialist that the amount of the award would be $5,000.00
instead of $2,500.00. However, during the second conversation, the Personnel
Specialist informed the Supervisory, Realty Specialist that the amount of the award
would not be $5,000.00. BLM noted that Ms. Sanderford was not informed of these
conversations. BLM stated that several weeks after these conversations,
Ms. Sanderford received a $5,000.00 award.
In her waiver request dated October 9, 2002, Ms. Sanderford provided the
following reasons in support of her request:
I relocated to the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Las Vegas Field
Office, Nevada, in November, 2001. As a result of that permanent
change of station and the successful sale of my private residence, I was
entitled to receive a Star Award in the amount of $2,500.00. I filed the
appropriate paperwork to obtain the monetary award of $2,500.00. It
was signed by my Supervisor and forwarded to the appropriate office at
the Nevada State Office (NSO) in Reno, Nevada, for processing. During
the approval process it was noted that the amount of this award
payment had been increased to $5,000.00 per BLM Washington Office
IM #2002-175. I was not aware of this change at the time I filed the
paperwork for the award. Any change to the amount of the award
submitted was made by someone other than me.
(Waiver Request at 1).
Ms. Sanderford explained that the overpayment was the result of an
administrative error caused by someone who decided that based on Instruction
Memorandum (IM) No. 2002-175 she should be given a $5,000.00 award rather
than a $2,500.00 award. She emphasized that the overpayment was not the result
of any action on her part.
By letter dated December 9, 2002, POD informed Ms. Sanderford that her
waiver request had been denied. On appeal, Ms. Sanderford asserted that the letter
denying her waiver request failed to address the applicable rules pertaining to the
26 OHA 32

D 2003-34
amount of the award in regard to IM No. 2002-175. She pointed out that the award
was specifically linked to the sale of her home and that IM No. 2002-175 increased
the amount of such awards from $2,500.00 to $5,000.00. Therefore, she believed
that the $5,000.00 award was proper.
By decision dated September 17, 2003, this Board affirmed POD’s denial of
Ms. Sanderford’s waiver request pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000) which authorizes
OHA to waive claims for overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity
and good conscience and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority
may not be exercised if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or
lack of good faith by the employee or any other person having an interest in
obtaining a waiver of the claim. See 344 DM 9 (1998). In our decision, we found
that Ms. Sanderford was not without fault in this matter because the record
demonstrated that she was aware of the overpayment. Ms. Sanderford stated in her
waiver request that she filed the appropriate paperwork to obtain the award of
$2,500.00. We found that when she received an award in the amount of $5,000.00,
rather than $2,500.00, she should have known that there had been an overpayment
and inquired as to the accuracy of the amount. We affirmed POD’s denial of
Ms. Sanderford’s waiver request based on the following:
Comptroller General decisions have held that if a reasonable person
would have inquired about the correctness of a payment, but the
employee did not, then the employee is not free from fault and the
claim may not be waived. Simon B. Guedea, B-189385, Aug. 10, 1977,
and cases cited. In these circumstances, it is clear that when
Ms. Sanderford received the $5,000.00 award, she knew that an over-
payment had occurred because she filed the paperwork for a $2,500.00
award. Where an employee was aware of the overpayment when it occurred,
a request for waiver will be denied. As a reasonable and prudent person who
knows that she is being overpaid, Ms. Sanderford should have set aside the
amount of overpayment for eventual refunding. In re Linda C. Mazzu,
17 OHA 108 (1999); Gilbert G. Quintero, B-183558, April 23, 1975. While
ideally no errors would occur in the payment process, such mistakes do occur
and Ms. Sanderford is not entitled to a windfall as a result.
In re Jane Sanderford, supra at 262.
26 OHA 33

D 2003-34
In her request for reconsideration, Ms. Sanderford referred to IM No. 2002-
175 dated May 20, 2002, and effective upon receipt. Attachment 1 to IM No. 2002-
175 provides answers to “Bureau of Land Management Permanent Change of Station
Frequently Asked Questions.” Provision No. 2 of Section II: Relocation Services
Contract states that a cash incentive award is available to an employee if the
employee sells his/her home without using the Relocation Services Contract.
Provision No. 2 provides that “[t]he State/Center Director will approve payment of
the cash incentive. The maximum relocation award amount is $5,000, and is raised
from $2,500 by this Instruction Memorandum.” Ms. Sanderford argued that at the
time she received her award, she was “in receipt” of IM No. 2002-175, and that it was
therefore reasonable for her to assume that the administrative office “had applied the
rule appropriately” as stated in IM No. 2002-175 and awarded her $5,000.00.
Ms. Sanderford stated that upon receipt of the award, she openly discussed the
award amount with her supervisors.
Ms. Sanderford asked that the Board consider the following two points:
First, was the rule properly applied or did I receive an incorrect
amount? Secondly, given that I was in receipt of the new instruction
memorandum, was it reasonable to assume the payment I received was
accurate. If I reasonably believed the payment was accurate, I request
acceptance of my waiver request.
(Request for Reconsideration, at 1).
In response to the first point, we note as we did in our September 17, 2003,
decision that it is not within the Board’s jurisdiction to interpret IM No. 2002-175
and to determine whether it was properly applied in Ms. Sanderford’s case. If
Ms. Sanderford was disputing the amount of her award, the matter would have been
properly considered pursuant to the Debt Collection Act of 1982, 5 U.S.C. § 5514
(2000). Under the provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA has authority to waive
an employee’s liability for debts arising from erroneous payments of pay, certain
allowances, and travel and transportation expenses when collection would be against
equity and good conscience and not in the best interests of the United States. This
waiver authority, however, applies only to claims arising out of “erroneous
payments.”
26 OHA 34

D 2003-34
If Ms. Sanderford believed that the $5,000.00 payment to her was the result of
administrative error as she indicated in her waiver request, then we have authority to
consider the matter under the waiver provisions as we did in our September 17,
2003, decision. In regard to her second point, Ms. Sanderford questioned whether it
was reasonable for her to assume that the $5,000.00 payment was accurate in light of
the fact that she had received a copy of the new instruction memorandum. Under the
circumstances, we find that it was not reasonable for Ms. Sanderford to make this
assumption. The attachment to IM No. 2002-175 provides that the maximum
relocation award amount is $5,000.00. Under this provision, Ms. Sanderford could
have been awarded any amount up to and including $5,000.00. When she received
the $5,000.00 payment instead of the $2,500.00 award for which she had filed, she
should have inquired as to whether the $5,000.00 amount was correct. Although
Ms. Sanderford stated that after receiving the award she openly discussed the amount
of the award with her supervisors, she did not state that she was told that the
$5,000.00 payment was correct. It was not reasonable for her to assume that the
$5,000.00 payment was correct based on IM No. 2002-175 without confirming this
assumption with her personnel office. See In re James D. Ration, 23 OHA 150, 153
(2003). Therefore, we find that Ms. Sanderford is not without fault in this matter,
and Bill for Collection No. Q2760014585 in the amount of $1,788.75 may not be
waived.
The general rules relating to procedures and practice before OHA are codified
at 43 CFR Part 4, Subpart B (2001). In order to be entitled to reconsideration of a
decision of an Ad Hoc Board, a petitioner is required by 43 CFR 4.21(d) (2001) to
show that "sufficient reason" exists for the Board to reconsider its decision, also
demonstrating that there exist "extraordinary circumstances" which justify reconsider-
ation. Under the standards and procedures for waivers set forth at 344 DM 9 (1998),
the request for reconsideration must demonstrate that the Director of OHA has
committed a material error of law or policy. 344 DM 9.6C (1998). After carefully
considering Ms. Sanderford’s petition for reconsideration, we conclude that she has
failed to demonstrate that sufficient reason and extraordinary circumstances exist for
reconsidering the Board's September 17, 2003, decision; nor has she shown that
there has been a material error of law or policy in this instance.
26 OHA 35

D 2003-34
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to this Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
by the Secretary of the Interior, 43 CFR 4.1, Ms. Sanderford’s petition to reconsider
the Board's September 17, 2003, decision affirming POD’s denial of Ms. Sanderford’s
waiver request is denied. The Board’s decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter. 344 DM 9 (1998).

OFFICE OF HEARINGS AND APPEALS
Office of the Director
801 N. Street, Suite 300
Arlington, Virginia 22203
Telephone (703) 235-3810 Facsimile (703) 235-9014
IN THE MATTER OF JAMES ANDERSON
(ON RECONSIDERATION)
Decided September 30, 2014
Motion for reconsideration of the opinion in Jn re James Anderson, 46 OHA 232
(2014), which vacated Administrative Wage Garnishment proceedings commenced by
the U.S. Department of the Treasury at the request of the Bureau of Land Management,
U.S. Department of the Interior.
Motion for Reconsideration granted; debt to the United States valid; underlying
opinion reversed.
APPEARANCES: Nancy S. Zahedi and Clementine Josephson, Office of the Solicitor,
Pacific Southwest Region, Sacramento, CA, for the Bureau of Land Management;
James Anderson, Winnemucca, NV, pro se.
OPINION BY HEARING OFFICIAL JOSHUA N. EPSTEIN
The undersigned vacated a Notice of Intent to Initiate Administrative Wage
Garnishment Proceedings (Garnishment Proceedings), which the U.S. Department of
the Treasury (Treasury) issued upon request of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), for the purposes of receiving from Appellant, James Anderson, trespass
penalties payments and cattle impoundment expenses. In re James Anderson, 46
232 (Feb. 7, 2014). The Garnishment Proceedings were vacated, and the debt to the
United States was found to be invalid, because BLM's submissions on the record failed
to demonstrate that, when it impounded Appellanf s cattle in January 2008, it had
complied with the Taylor Grazing Act impoundment notification regulations. BLM's
had not made an appearance in the underlying Garnishment
a Motion for Reconsideration ("Motion"). Therein, BLM put forth
a "fuller record and background," and argued that the Garnishment Proceedings were
erroneously vacated based on incorrect "inferences or interpretations of the record."
Motion at 2.
The facts of the case were summarized, as necessary, in the underlying decision,
and will not be presented herein. As a general practice in Office of Hearings and
Appeals (OHA) proceedings, "reconsideration" may be granted, but only upon a
47 OHA 94

showing of "extraordinary circumstances." 43 C.F.R. § 4.21(d). 1 Extraordinary
circumstances exist where, among other things, the party seeking reconsideration
shows that the underlying decision was based on an erroneous "premise." See
(On Reconsideration), 159 (2003).2 Such a premise was made in
the underlying decision, as discussed below.
The underlying BLM failed to establish the debt's
premised on the "determin[ation] that BLM did not demonstrate compliance with the
Act's impounding notification requirements." 46 OHA at 235. Under the notice
requirements, and as discussed in the decision, BLM must provide either direct notice
or public notice. 43 C.F.R. § 4150.4-l(a)-(b). The type of notice due depends on
BLM's knowledge, or lack of knowledge, of who owns the unauthorized livestock at
issue. If ownership is known, direct notice is necessary; if ownership is unknown,
public notice is sufficient. Id. In the Garnishment Proceedings, BLM provided no
evidence of direct notice, so it was left with only the option of showing compliance via
public notice. BLM stated that public notice was made in December month
prior to the this was found to be insufficient because, as a
threshold matter, BLM had offered no statement that it lacked knowledge of who
owned the cattle. Further, BLM had also provided evidence that earlier in
well as in had issued to Appellant trespass notices pertaining to unpermitted
grazing activities at the same allotment at issue.
The Motion for Reconsideration contains facts that, as a matter of logic, correct
the underlying decision's premise that BLM failed to comply with the impoundment
notice requirements via public notice. BLM has now submitted threshold evidence
that it lacked knowledge of Appellant's ownership. Specifically, through a Declaration
from the District Office Rangeland Management Specialist, BLM has established that it
"was not aware that [Appellant] had trespass cattle on the public range" at the time of
The reconsideration standard in section 4.21(d) appears in 43 C.F.R. Subpart B,
which establishes OHA's "General Rules Relating to Procedures and Practice." These
general rules are "applicable to all types of proceedings" in OHA. 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b).
Further, section 4.21(d) applies "unless otherwise provided by regulation." The
regulations containing Treasury's administrative wage garnishment hearings
procedures contain no reconsideration standard that would otherwise apply. 31
C.F.R. §
In Tiegen, the Interior Board of Land Appeals cited C.F.R. § 4.403, the
reconsideration standard codified among "Special Rules Applicable to Public Land
Hearings and Appeals." 43 C.F.R. Subpart E. Section 4.403, however, contains the
same "extraordinary circumstances" test for obtaining reconsideration that section
4.21(d) does.
47 OHA 95

the impoundment. Declaration at 12. Further, BLM also added that Appellant had
responded to BLM's 2007 trespass notice by informing BLM that he would be removing
his livestock from the closed allotment as of April 2007. Id. at 4. With this new
evidence, BLM has now accounted for its knowledge of Appellant's recent trespass
history and explained why, despite that knowledge, it lacked particular knowledge of
the trespass referenced in its December 2007 public notice. 3
Based on the foregoing, it is determined that BLM's Motion offers new evidence,
presented in a light demonstrating a fundamental error in a main premise of the
underlying decision. In light of extraordinary circumstances shown, reconsideration
is hereby granted. Further, with this new evidence, BLM has established compliance
with the impoundment notice requirements. 4 Therefore, BLM has now shown a
proper basis for the penalties and expenses sought from Appellant, and Appellant's
debt to the United States is found to be valid. As a result, the underlying decision is
reversed.5
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 31 C.F.R. § 285.11(f)(12).
Joshua N. Epstein
Hearing Official
The Motion also addresses a BLM official's statement, made to Appellant after the
impoundment had occurred, that Appellant was free to reclaim his cattle because BLM
had not obtained a court order. In the underlying decision, that statement was seen as
a factor making it even less certain that the penalties and expenses were valid. But
because this factor was not the fundamental premise upon
which the underlying decision was made was that BLM failed to comply with the
impoundment notice is not necessary to consider whether the
Motion's explanation for BLM's lack of a court order too warrants that reconsideration
be granted.
Appellant was provided an opportunity to respond to the Motion, but did not respond.
BLM is reminded of its willingness to "discuss a reasonable settlement and
compromise of [Appellant's] debt." Motion at 11 n.3.
47 OHA 96

court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 16 OHA 115 — IN RE MILLARD
text:
IN THE MATTER OF ROBERT L. AND
ERMA P. MILLARD
D-98-54 Decided July 28, 1998
Appeal from a decision of the Yuma, Arizona, Field Office, Bureau of Land
Management, terminating residential occupancy permit on Federal lands. CAAZCA 23502.
Affirmed.
1. Cabin Sites: Public Conservation and Recreation Areas
BLM properly terminates a permit for a private residence site on
public land on the lower Colorado River where the permit provided
for a year to year occupancy and was subject to termination on
notice at the end of any year's period, and where BLM's land use
planning showed that the public interest would be best served by
opening the area to public recreational access.
APPEARANCES: Robert and Erma Millard, pro sese; Richard R. Greenfield, Esq., Office of
the Field Solicitor, U. S. Department of the Interior, Phoenix, Arizona, for the Bureau of
Land Management.
OPINION BY WOLFGANG E. NEUDORFER
Robert and Erma Millard (Appellants) have appealed from a February 5, 1998 decision
of the Yuma, Arizona, Field Office, Bureau of Land Management (BLM), providing notice of
termination, and terminating their residential occupancy permit CAAZCA 23502 effective
December 31, 1998. Appellants have also petitioned for a stay pending a decision on appeal.
The land covered by the permit is Parcel WC-23, consisting of 0.19 acres 15 miles south of
Palo Verde, Imperial County, California, on the west bank of the Colorado River.
Background
The BLM's Yuma, Arizona, Field office, formerly the Lower Colorado Land Use
Office, was established in 1961 by Secretarial Order No. 2854 to eliminate trespass
occupancy along the lower Colorado River corridor, on lands withdrawn by the Bureau of
Reclamation. In the 1960's, that office issued residential occupancy permits to temporarily
16 OHA 115

resolve trespass occupancies along the river. The permits legalized trespass occupancies on
Federal land on a year-to-year basis and were subject to termination when other needs for the
land were identified. Thus, the permit issued to Appellants provides at paragraph 5 that it
was to run for successive one-year periods and could be terminated at the end of any such
period "by written notice served by the United States upon the applicant at least ninety (90)
days in advance thereof." The permit further provided, at paragraph 8, that the granting
thereof did not confer "any title to or property interest in any of the lands within the permit
area, nor * * * any right to renew or extend the permit beyond the period provided for in
paragraph 5 hereof." Paragraph 16 provided that all of the rights of the permittee would
cease upon the termination of the permit.
Beginning in the 1960's the Department developed and implemented various land use
plans for the Colorado River. In 1964, the Lower Colorado River Land Use Plan established
long range proposals for recreational use along the river. In 1975 the La Paz Management
Framework Plan carried forward and expanded earlier planning decisions. This was followed
in 1975 by the Ehrenberg-Cibola Recreation Management Plan, the Yuma District Resource
Management Plan of 1986, and the Ehrenberg-Cibola Recreation Area Management plan of
1994 (RAMP). The Yuma District Management Plan specifically states that existing
residential permits would be phased out and associated improvements removed. The purpose
of this land use planning was to open the area up for recreational access by the general public.
Over the years, the BLM provided ample notice to permittees that the lands were
needed and that their permits would be terminated. By letters of September 17, 1973, March
6, 1992, February 28, 1995, and September 27, 1996, the BLM provided notice that the
permits would be phased out and invited permittees to participate in the planning process for
the lands. BLM also published notice of its intention to implement the Ehrenberg-Cibola
RAMP. 59 Fed. Reg. 18151 (Apr. 15, 1994).
Arguments of the Parties
The Appellants contend that BLM has no explicit reason for terminating the permits,
and that there are no tangible or formal concrete plans for the construction of improvements
to require the termination of their permit. Appellants note that under the original permitting
scheme, permits were to be granted until there was another specific use for the property.
Appellants contend that no specific other use for the property is contemplated.
The Appellants refer to the Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP noting that it outlines a plan for a
recreational facility including a fishing pier and a parking lot embracing the their permit area.
Appellants assert that there are no plans to construct this facility, only vague future
possibilities.
The Appellants recite that oral inquiries made of employees of various agencies,
including the Fish and Wildlife Service, revealed a lack of knowledge, on the part of these
16 OHA 116

employees, as to plans for the recreational development outlined in the RAMP. Appellants
note that the RAMP does not specifically indicate that their permit area will actually interfere
with thed parking lot and fishing pier. Appellants contend that there is little use of the area
by recreationists and that expansion is unnecessary.
The Appellants request that BLM continue to extend their permit until the land they
occupy will be used for a specific purpose at a specific time.
The BLM 1/ points out the limitations of the permits under which Appellants occupy
the site. BLM asserts that termination of the permit, with ample notice, is fully consistent
with BLM's responsibility for managing the public lands as exercised in the development of
the various land management plans covering the area.
Counsel for BLM has submitted the affidavit of Joy Gilbert, a senior technical
specialist in the Yuma Field Office, who manages the special permitting program on the
lower Colorado River corridor. Gilbert states in her affidavit that the Millards' permit site is
one of the few remaining private permits, is in a prime waterfront recreation use area and is
inconsistent with opening the area for use by the public (Id., at 4.)
Gilbert further states that BLM plans to install a fishing pier at the site of the
residential permits at Walter's Camp (the area in which the Millards' site is located), and that
plans for the site are set forth in the Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP (Id., at 8, 9.)
Counsel for BLM concludes that terminating the Millards' permit was a proper use of
BLM's discretionary authority and that the Millards have shown no error of fact or law in the
BLM determination.
Discussion
[1] The Ehrenberg-Cibola RAMP covers a special recreation management area
embracing approximately 209,410 acres of land along the Colorado River in western Arizona
and southeastern California. BLM administers 114,050 acres of this land. The objective of
the RAMP is to “provide the public with a broad base of recreational activities within an
enjoyable recreational setting * * * to enhance the facilities and services through improved
__________________________
1/ Counsel for BLM asserts in his answer that neither the Millard's notice of appeal nor their
statement of reasons was served on his Phoenix, Arizona, office. The regulations pertaining
to ad hoc appeals provide for the mailing, by an appellant, of a notice of appeal and statement
of reasons "to the Departmental official whose action or decision is being appealed." The
Millards' notice of appeal and statement of reasons indicate that copies were served on the
BLM's Yuma Field Office. 43 C.F.R. § 4.701.
16 OHA 117

facility design, development of interpretive areas, brochures and maps, and increased Bureau
of Land Management (BLM) presence.” (RAMP at 1.)
The RAMP states that the Walter's Camp area was identified by the public during
scoping meetings "as an ideal location for a fishing pier." The planning goal is to “[p]rovide
a universally accessible facility for all users to access the waters of the Colorado River for
pier fishing in an area that has limited opportunities for this type of fishing activity.”
The RAMP states that the "Concept" is to develop a public recreational facility which
will meet all accessibility criteria and will include a parking area and fishing pier (RAMP at
34.)
As noted earlier, notice of the RAMP was published in 59 Fed. Reg. 18151 (Apr. 15,
1994). That notice summarized important aspects of the RAMP and provided a 30-day
appeal period.
Section 102 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) 43
U.S.C. § 1701(a)(2) (1994) states that the national interest will be best realized if the present
and future use of the public lands "is projected through a land use planning process
coordinated with other Federal and State planning efforts." Section 202, 43 U.S.C. § 1712,
invests the Secretary with the authority to develop, maintain, and revise land use plans.
A regulation applicable to this appeal, 43 C.F.R. § 21.4 (a)(2), provides:
Whenever the Authorized Officer determines that the public need for use
of a recreation or conservation area has grown to a point where continued private
cabin site use is no longer in the public interest, the procedures set forth in
paragraph (b) of this section will be invoked to phase out existing permits by
reducing and eliminating renewals, or extensions, consistent with protection of
legitimate investment in improvements. [2/]
Having reviewed the Appellants' arguments in light of the above authorities, we
conclude that BLM's determination to terminate the Millards' permit is proper and must be
sustained. Appellants' rights of occupancy are, in the first instance, clearly defined by the
permit itself. That permit circumscribed their occupancy as one from year to year,
specifically excluded title to or property interest in the permitted land, and provided for
termination on notice at the end of such 1-year periods. Furthermore, the terms of the permit
did not oblige the grantor to provide specific reasons for termination or non-renewal. Thus,
__________________________
2/ 43 C.F.R. § 21.4 (b) provides guidelines for protection of investments in improvements.
16 OHA 118

even in absence the extensive justification provided by this record for termination of the
permit, Appellants have no legal or equitable right for its continuance. Therefore, the facts
that, as Appellants argue, neither a time certain nor construction specifications are in place
for the fishing pier or parking lot are not a bar to the BLM's termination of the permit.
Nevertheless, the regulation quoted above does provide that termination of occupancy
sites such as the Millards' should be attended by a determination of the public interest. The
record in this case amply demonstrates that the public interest will best be served by
termination of the private occupancy permits to make way for greater public recreational
opportunities. The weighing of the public interest in public land use determinations is
committed to the sound discretion of the BLM and its experts. As members of the public,
Appellants may participate in BLM's land use planning and may appeal certain planning
decisions. However, their disagreement with such decisions, while understandable, provides
no cause for reversal in the absence of a showing of error.
In administrative proceedings before the Department, the general rule is that there be
proof by a preponderance of the evidence that a decision is in error if an appellant is to
prevail. Bender v. Clark, 744 F.2d 1424 (10th Cir. 1984). Thus, in order to prevail in a
challenge to a BLM decision granting or denying applications to use Federal lands, the
challenging party must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the BLM erred
in reaching its conclusion. Appellants have made no such showing and the record herein
supports the BLM's decision.
Therefore, pursuant to the authority delegated to the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals by the
Secretary of the Interior, 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(4), the decision appealed from is affirmed and
the request for stay is denied.
____________________________
Wolfgang E. Neudorfer
Member, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
I concur:
__________________________
Charles E. Breece
Chairman, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
16 OHA 119

title: 33 OHA 174 — IN RE ROBINSON
text:
September 20, 2006
IN THE MATTER OF : Docket No. D 2005-93
DONALD E. ROBINSON :
: Waiver Request
:
: Waiver Request Granted
ORDER
On September 23, 2005, Sue Bylsma, Supervisor, Taxes and Collections
Group, Payroll Operations Division (POD), National Business Center, Office of the
Secretary, Denver, Colorado, filed with the Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) a
request for waiver of salary overpayments submitted by Donald E. Robinson, an
employee of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), in the amount of $1,735.00,
Bill for Collection No. 50880720594.
The record shows that the overpayment was discovered on March 1, 2005, and
Mr. Robinson was notified of its existence on March 1, 2005. POD prepared an
Administrative Report which accompanied Mr. Robinson’s request and explained the
circumstances of the salary overpayment as follows:
Mr. Donald Robinson, an employee of the Bureau of Land Management
(BLM), received erroneous overpayments of salary due to the miscoding
of his Position Title Code. Employee was coded as “AA” and should
have been coded as “LE”. This error affects the calculation of the FLSA
premium. Mr. Robinson occupies a law enforcement position, and
receives Administratively Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO). AUO
employees are expected to work an average of 2 ¾ hours weekly of
uncontrollable overtime. The FLSA premium is calculated on all actual
hours worked minus 42 ¾ hours weekly or 85 ½ biweekly. The error
continued from pay period (PP) 2003-03 through 2005-06. This bill of
collection pertains to PP 2004-07 through 2005-06.
(Administrative Report, POD 2005-125, at 1.)
33 OHA 174

D 2005-93
POD included a summary of the statement of the office involved as follows:
The BLM Human Resources Office submitted a waiver request on behalf
of Mr. Robinson stating that in a Briefing Paper prepared by the Bureau
of Land Management’s Office of Law Enforcement and Security,
Mr. Robinson was identified as being in the incorrect Position Title Code.
He was coded as “AA” and should have been coded as “LE”.
BLM states that this coding does not appear anywhere on the
Notification of Personnel Action, Time and Attendance Reports or Leave
and Earning Statements. Mr. Robinson could not have known that this
code affected his salary nor could he have known he was coded
incorrectly.
BLM did not notify Mr. Robinson regarding the correction because at
the time the correction was made, they did not anticipate the change
affecting his salary. BLM feels strongly that making Mr. Robinson pay
back the overpayment based on an administrative error unknown to
him would be unreasonable. There is no indication of any
misrepresentation, fraud, or lack of good faith of the employee.
(Administrative Report, POD 2005-125, at 1-2.)
In his August 18, 2005, request for waiver, Mr. Robinson indicated that the
“Position Title Code” did not appear on any of his personnel documents and he had
no reason to recognize the error in that code. Mr. Robinson stated that he has made
“no misrepresentation, fraud, or lack of good faith in determining that [his] pay was
correct.”
POD provided the following findings and conclusions regarding
Mr. Robinson’s request for waiver:
Waivers of claims for overpayment of wages may be granted under
5 U.S.C. 5584, when collection would be against equity and good
conscience and not in the best interests of the United States, unless
there is indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good
faith on the employee’s part. We find no indication of the above in this
matter.
The Comptroller General has consistently held that an employee is not
entitled to a waiver as a matter of legal right whenever they receive an
overpayment through an administrative error. Instead, the standards
implementing the waiver statute state, in general, waiver is precluded
33 OHA 175

D 2005-93
when an employee receives a significant unexplained increase in pay or
allowances, or otherwise knows, or reasonably should know, that an
erroneous payment has occurred and fails to make inquiries or bring
the matter to the attention of the appropriate officials.
The issue in this case is whether Mr. Robinson can be said to be at
“fault” in this matter as that term is used in the statute. Ordinarily,
fault may be imputed to an employee if there is anything in the record
sufficient to indicate that employee knew or should have known about
the overpayment and failed to question it. In deciding this, we ask
whether a reasonable person in the employee’s position should have
been aware that they were receiving more salary payment than they
were entitled to. If so, the employee had the obligation to set aside the
overpayment and hold it for repayment to the Government when the
error was corrected. (CG Decision No. B-259124).
We find that Mr. Robinson was unaware of the Position Title Code error
and that he was receiving erroneous overpayments of salary. There is
nothing in the record to indicate that Mr. Robinson could have known
that this code affected his salary. CG Decision No. B-206674 states in
general, that waiver of overpayments is granted where the agency
improperly fixed employee’s rate, and it appeared that the employee
was not familiar with pay regulations, and was not furnished with pay
or personnel records which, if examined, would have led to the
discovery of the error. Therefore, we do not find Mr. Robinson at fault
in this matter and recommend approval of the request for waiver by his
agency on his behalf.
(Administrative Report, POD 2005-125, at 2.)
OHA exercises the Secretary of the Interior’s delegated authority to waive
collection of erroneous payments over $1,500 from employees of the Department of
the Interior and its constituent bureaus. POD has authority to waive debts of less
than $1,500 arising out of erroneous payments under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). If
POD denies a waiver request, an appeal can be made to this office.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA is authorized to waive claims for
overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity and good conscience
and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority may not be exercised
if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good faith by the
employee or any other person having an interest in obtaining a waiver of the claim.
344 DM 9. Waiver determinations under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000) are based solely on
33 OHA 176

D 2005-93
the facts and circumstances giving rise to the erroneous payment and the employee’s
knowledge or fault in the matter. See, e.g., In re Fred M. Ritchhart,
18 OHA 47, 49 (1999). In the instant case, it is undisputed that the erroneous salary
overpayments made to Mr. Robinson occurred as the result of administrative error.
It is well settled by decisions of the Comptroller General that where an
employee was aware, or should have been aware, of an overpayment of pay when it
occurred, the employee cannot reasonably expect to retain such payments, but should
set them aside and expect the Government to seek recovery. Additionally, the
employee should make provision for repayment of the overpayments. Bruce C.
Hanson, B-260849, September 19, 1995. In these circumstances, the employee is not
entitled to relief under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). In such cases, collection of an
overpayment is not considered to be against equity, good conscience, or contrary to
the best interests of the United States. See Joan R. Edwards, B-271616, October 3,
1996; Sandra L. Geer, B-243686, July 2, 1991; L. Mitchell Dick, B-192283,
November 15, 1978.
As noted by POD, the issue in this case is whether Mr. Robinson can be said to
be at fault in this matter as that term is used in the statute. The standard employed
by the Comptroller General and OHA is to determine whether a reasonable person
should have been aware that he was receiving a payment to which he was not
entitled. Where the reasonable person would have made inquiry, but the employee
did not, then he is not free from fault and the claim cannot be waived. John H.
Young, Jr., B-253640, November 4, 1993. In this case, as indicated in the record,
Mr. Robinson’s pay and personnel records would not have alerted him to the fact that
an error had occurred. Generally, where an employee has documentary records, such
as Forms SF-50 (Notification of Personnel Action) and L&E (Leave and Earnings)
statements, and fails to review those documents for accuracy or otherwise fails to
take corrective action, he is not without fault and waiver will be denied. John H.
Young, Jr., supra; Gordon Field, M.D., B-224910, June 22, 1987. Comptroller
General decisions have held that if a reasonable person would have inquired about
the correctness of a payment, but the employee did not, then the employee is not free
from fault and the claim may not be waived. Simon B. Guedea, B-189385,
August 10, 1997, and cases cited. Further, fault exists if, in light of all the facts, it is
determined that an employee exercising reasonable diligence should have known that
an error existed and would have taken action to see to it that the error was corrected.
In re Mary Ann Slim, 18 OHA 57, 58-59 (1999). We find that the record in this case
does not support a finding that Mr. Robinson failed to exercise reasonable diligence
in reviewing his personnel documents. Therefore, he is entitled to a waiver of this
debt.
33 OHA 177

D 2005-93
In summary, on the basis of the record before us, we find that Mr. Robinson is
not at fault in this matter, and that it would be against equity and good conscience
and the best interests of the United States to deny his request for waiver of Bill for
Collection No. 50880720594 in the amount of $1,735.00. Accordingly, the waiver
request submitted by Mr. Robinson is hereby granted.
Pursuant to 344 DM 9, this decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter.
_______________________________
Teresa M. Garrity
Chair, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
I concur:
James L. Byrnes
Member, Ad Hoc Board of Appeals
33 OHA 178

court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 45 OHA 158 — IN RE WATTS
text:
IN THE MATTER OF LINDA WATTS
DIR-2012-0032 Decided March 7, 2013
Appeal from a determination made by a Board of Survey, Oregon State Office,
Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Portland, Oregon, finding employee, Linda
Watts, financially liable for the loss of government equipment due to negligence.
Report of Survey No. ORBRS11-002.
Reversed.
1. Property Board of Survey: Negligence
For the Ad Hoc Board of Appeals to affirm a Board of Survey’s
determination of employee liability in simple negligence, the
record must show that the loss of property was the result of the
employee’s failure to exercise the degree of care in which a
prudent person would exercise under like circumstances.
APPEARANCES: Linda Watts, Hines, Oregon, pro se.
OPINION BY CHAIRMAN JOSUHA N. EPSTEIN
Introduction
Appellant, Linda Watts, a BLM employee in the Burns District Office, Hines,
Oregon, has appealed the January 31, 2012, decision of the Reviewing Authority
affirming the determination of the Board of Survey, BLM, Oregon State Office,
Portland, Oregon (Board), which found Appellant negligent and financially liable for
loss of Government property—a Trimble Juno SB Handheld Global Positioning
System, Serial No. 41000093100339 (Property No. L0522487 Asset 84667) (property
or GPS). The loss occurred on June 14, 2010, when Appellant was performing a
weed survey in a fuel treatment unit. The Board assessed $250.00 in damages, and
Appellant received notice of the decision via a January 31, 2012, memorandum from
Jason Moss, Property Utilization Specialist, National Operations Center, Denver,
Colorado.
The Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) received the appeal on February
27, 2012, and the appeal is therefore timely. 43 C.F.R. § 4.701. OHA has assigned
45 OHA 158

DIR-2012-0032
the above-captioned docket number to the matter and obtained BLM’s official file. Id.
at § 4.702. Therefore, the matter is ready for disposition.
The Board of Survey Decision
Appellant provided an initial statement on a “Missing/Damaged Property”
form:
On June 14th, I was using the [GPS] for navigation and weed
survey in . . . a fuels unit . . . . As there was no place to secure the unit
to the ATV and navigate drive [sic] the ATV at the same time, I had unit
on the seat. I last used unit on NE side of unit to see where I was
within the unit and then started looking for a way to the road East of
unit, when I got to the road, noticed unit was gone.
Appellant’s “Missing/Damaged Property” statement, dated January 24, 2011.
Appellant supplemented that initial statement by informing the Board that her
office had started “working on a way to attach GPS units to the ATV’s [sic].”
Appellant’s Letter to Board of Survey Chairperson, May 11, 2011.
The Board made the following Findings and Determinations:
On 06/14/2010 Ms. Watts was conducting weed surveys on an
ATV in a fuel treatment unit. In the course of her work she was using a
GPS unit for navigation and site locations. As there was no means to
attach the GPS unit to the ATV she set it down on the seat as she
negotiated her way out of the unit. When she reached the road she
noticed it was missing. A number of attempts were made to recover the
unit.
Employees have a responsibility to safeguard Government
property from damage and loss. Ms. Watts failed to exercise due
diligence by not securing the unit to her persons [sic] as there was no
means to attach it to the ATV. Each individual is normally and
regularly responsible for using whatever means available to secure
small, valuable too [sic] their person in order to avoid loss.
The board finds that there was SIMPLE NEGLIGENCE on the
part of Ms. Watts. This will result in and assessment of financial
responsibility of $250.00 for the [loss of the Government property].
Findings and Determinations, ORBRS11-0002.
45 OHA 159

DIR-2012-0032
The Board received concurrence from the Deputy Regional Solicitor in
the Department of the Interior’s Pacific Northwest Region. That official found
that Appellant “failed to safeguard her equipment,” and that such conduct
“resulted in the loss of the equipment.” Memorandum from Deputy Regional
Solicitor, dated Oct. 25, 2011.
Argument on Appeal
Appellant has provided the following statement to this Board:
On June 14, 2010, I was using the [GPS] unit for navigation and
weed survey in . . . a fuels unit . . . . As there was no place to secure
the unit to the [ATV], navigate and drive the ATV at the same time, I
placed the unit on the seat between my legs. I last used the unit on the
northeast side of the fuels unit to check my location, and then started
looking for a way through the juniper, brush, and boulders to a road . .
. . When I arrived at the road the GPS unit was gone. Caryn Meinicke
(another Bureau of Land Management employee) and I back-tracked
my path and did an extensive search from the road back through the
fuels unit. Do [sic] to the dense Shrub cover, the color and small size
of the GPS unit, it was not located. The GPS unit had a black protective
“otter box” of which covered most of the bright yellow on the unit and
blended well with the surrounding rocks and shade of the brush.
On June 18, 2010, I went back with the SWAT crew and
searched for the GPS unit again.
In September, 2010, Caryn went back and did another search for
the GPS unit.
Tim Newkirk, Burns District Forester, asked his cutters to keep
an eye out for the GPS unit, when they were . . . in the fuels unit.
The Determinations stated that the GPS unit should have been
attached to my person; however I had no way to attach the GPS to
either the ATV or my person and still use it to navigate through the
fuels unit.
Appeal, dated February 23, 2012.
Appellant has also provided the following supporting statement from the
Burns District Office Manager:
45 OHA 160

DIR-2012-0032
On June 14, 2010 Linda Watts, an employee on our district, was
performing routine field work and inadvertently lost the Global
Positioning System (GPS) unit she was using to navigate and collect
data. Despite many attempts to locate the unit, it was not found.
After reviewing the situation with the employee and her field
supervisor, I determined that the Bureau of Land Management Burns
District had not provided adequate means to secure the GPS unit.
Following that incident, the weed program purchased brackets designed
to secure the GPS units while using them to navigate in the field.
While I regret the loss of the equipment, I do not believe it was
negligence on the part of the employee but rather inadequate means to
secure the equipment which was to blame.
I believe the employee had secured the GPS unit as best she
could under the circumstances . . . . I am prepared to accept the loss of
the equipment as an unfortunate learning experience which has already
led to greatly improved methods for securing our GPS property.
Memorandum from District Office Manager Brendan Cain, dated Feb. 24,
2012.
Review of the Survey Decision
[1] Without question, the Government has suffered a property loss. The
particular issue here is whether the Board properly concluded that the GPS was lost
due to simple negligence by the Appellant. 410 DM 114-60.808-1(b)(2). Simple
negligence involves “an act or omission of the employee in which he/she failed to
exercise the degree of care, precaution, attention, and vigilance which a prudent
person would exercise under like circumstances.” Id. Regardless of whether an
accident or loss occurs, this Office may find an employee liable only if the record
“convincingly demonstrate[s] . . . that the employee acted in an imprudent manner.”
410 DM 114-60.808-1(a). As this Office has stated, a Board’s negligence finding
must be based on more than cursory findings and conclusions. In re Victoria
Hartman, 42 OHA 96, 99 (2011).
Here, we cannot affirm the Board’s simple negligence finding. The Board
determined that Appellant had a duty to use available means to secure small and
valuable property such as the GPS. Board of Survey Findings and Determinations,
OBRS11-0002. It failed to identify, however, any means that actually were available
to her. As a result, there is no basis for concluding that Appellant’s conduct
constituted a failure to meet the duty that the Board found applicable.
45 OHA 161

DIR-2012-0032
Similarly, the Board also relied on a BLM memorandum stating that employees
working in the field must “inventory equipment frequently.” Burns District Office
Memorandum, dated Oct. 1, 2010; see also Memorandum from Deputy Regional
Solicitor. Appellant stated that she checked for the property upon exiting a shrub-
covered area and reaching a road. Appeal at 1. The Board did not establish the
frequency with which Appellant should have inventory-checked the GPS and, as a
result, identified no basis for concluding that Appellant checked too late, or less
frequently than she ought to have. See In re Kevin C. O’Reilly, 31 OHA 16, 23-24
(2005) (negligence finding reversed where employee lost keys in backcountry despite
reasonable attempts to meet requirement that he secure them to his person at all
times). Nevertheless, even if there was a basis to conclude that Appellant did not
make sufficient efforts to safeguard the GPS unit while working in the field, the
Board cited no evidence that the property was lost as a result of her effort, or lack
thereof. See In re Scott L. Meneely, 39 OHA 287, 292 (2009) (negligence finding
reversed due to a Board of Survey’s “mere speculation” that a failure to meet a duty
resulted in the property loss).
We hereby reverse the Board’s finding of simple negligence and grant the
appeal. Appellant is not financially liable for the loss of the Trimble Juno SB GPS
unit. 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(3).
This decision constitutes the final administrative determination of the
Department in this matter. 43 C.F.R. § 4.1(b)(3), 410 DM 60.808-7.

title: 38 OHA 68 — IN RE NAYLOR
text:
January 29, 2009
IN THE MATTER OF ) Docket No. D 2008-10
LAIRD P. NAYLOR )
) Waiver Request
)
) Waiver Request Granted
ORDER
On November 6, 2007, Sue Bylsma, Supervisor, Taxes and Collections Group,
Payroll Operations Division (POD), National Business Center, Office of the Secretary,
Denver, Colorado, filed with the Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) a request for
waiver of salary overpayments submitted by Laird P. Naylor, an employee of the
Bureau of Land Management (BLM), in the total amount of $12,332.92, Bill for
Collection No. M0723200005 (for $10,768.01) and Bill for Collection No.
71980065479 (for $1,564.91).
The record shows that the overpayment was discovered in June 2007, and
Laird P. Naylor was notified of its existence in June 2007. POD prepared an
Administrative Report which accompanied Mr. Naylor’s request and explained the
circumstances of the salary overpayment as follows:
Mr. Laird Naylor, an employee of the Bureau of Land
Management (BLM), received erroneous overpayments of salary due to
the miscoding of his FLSA Class. A personnel action was processed
correcting employee’s FLSA status from non-exempt to exempt. This
correction reduced Mr. Naylor’s overtime rate, which should have been
capped at the GS-10, Step 1 pay.
Administrative Report, RA200700191, at 1.
POD included a summary of the statement of the office involved as follows:
The BLM Human Resources Office submitted a statement stating
that Mr. Naylor was reassigned from [the] National Park Service to
38 OHA 68

D 2008-10
[the] Bureau of Land Management on March 28, 1999 and all SF-50’s
were erroneously coded to non-exempt dated up until January 7, 2007.
BLM further states that Mr. Naylor was unaware of the error
until he was informed by them in June of 2007. Mr. Naylor was not
provided with documents which if reviewed would have alerted him to
the fact that an error had occurred.
Id. at 2.
POD provided the following findings and conclusions regarding Mr. Laird’s
request for waiver:
Waivers of claims for overpayment of wages may be granted
under 5 U.S.C. 5584, when collection would be against equity and good
conscience and not in the best interests of the United States, unless
there is indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good
faith on the employee’s part. We find no indication of the above in this
matter.
The Comptroller General has consistently held that an employee
is not entitled to a waiver as a matter of legal right whenever they
receive an overpayment through an administrative error. Instead, the
standards implementing the waiver statute state, in general, waiver is
precluded when an employee receives a significant unexplained
increase in pay or allowances, or otherwise knows, or reasonably
should know, that an erroneous payment has occurred and fails to
make inquiries or bring the matter to the attention of the appropriate
officials.
The issue in this case is whether Mr. Naylor can be said to be at
"fault" in this matter as that term is used in the statute. Ordinarily, fault
may be imputed to an employee if there is anything in the record
sufficient to indicate that employee knew or should have known about
the overpayment and failed to question it. In deciding this, we ask
whether a reasonable person in the employee's position should have
been aware that they were receiving more salary payment than they
were entitled to. If so, the employee had the obligation to set aside the
overpayment and hold it for repayment to the Government when the
error was corrected. (CG Decision No. B-259124, Feb. 23, 1995).
38 OHA 69

D 2008-10
We find that in this case, there is nothing in the record to
indicate that the employee knew or should have known that an error
had occurred. Mr. Naylor’s pay and personnel records would not have
alerted him to the fact that an error had occurred. Generally, where an
employee has documentary records, such as SF-50 (Notification of
Personnel Action) and L&E (Leave and Earnings) statements, and fails
to review those documents for accuracy or otherwise fails to take
corrective action, he is not without fault and waiver will be denied.
The record in this case indicates that Mr. Naylor’s personnel records
continually displayed that he was a non-exempt employee for FLSA
purposes. Overtime pay and FLSA status are complicated matters and
Mr. Naylor cannot be presumed to have knowledge of the rules and
regulations governing their applicability to him.
CG Decision No. B-206674 states in general, that waiver of
overpayments is granted where the agency improperly fixed employee’s
rate, and it appeared that the employee was not familiar with the pay
regulations, and was not furnished with pay or personnel records
which, if examined, would have led to the discovery of the error.
Therefore, we do not find Mr. Naylor at fault in this matter and
recommend approval of his request for waiver.
Id. at 2-3.
OHA exercises the Secretary of the Interior’s delegated authority to waive
collection of erroneous payments over $1,500 from employees of the Department of
the Interior and its constituent bureaus. POD has authority to waive debts of less
than $1,500 arising out of erroneous payments under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). If
POD denies a waiver request, an appeal can be made to this Office.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA is authorized to waive claims for
overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity and good conscience
and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority may not be exercised
if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good faith by the
employee or any other person having an interest in obtaining a waiver of the claim.
See 344 DM 9. Waiver determinations under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000) are based solely
on the facts and circumstances giving rise to the erroneous payment and the
employee’s knowledge or fault in the matter. See, e.g., In re Fred M. Ritchhart,
18 OHA 47, 49 (1999). In the instant case, it is undisputed that the erroneous salary
overpayments made to Mr. Naylor occurred as the result of administrative error.
38 OHA 70

D 2008-10
It is well settled by decisions of the Comptroller General that where an
employee was aware, or should have been aware, of an overpayment of pay when it
occurred, the employee cannot reasonably expect to retain such payments, but should
set them aside and expect the Government to seek recovery. Additionally, the
employee should make provision for repayment of the overpayments. Bruce C.
Hanson, B-260849, September 19, 1995. In these circumstances, the employee is not
entitled to relief under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). In such cases, collection of an
overpayment is not considered to be against equity, good conscience, or contrary to
the best interests of the United States. See Joan R. Edwards, B-271616, October 3,
1996; Sandra L. Geer, B-243686, July 2, 1991; L. Mitchell Dick, B-192283,
November 15, 1978.
Waiver is not proper if the employee was aware that he had received an
overpayment. Amadeo Martinez, Jr., B-261628, June 13, 1996. Decisions of the
Comptroller General state that where an agency notifies an employee of an
overpayment, the employee is on notice and precluded from relying on the accuracy
of the overpayment. In such cases, waiver is not appropriate since collection of the
overpayment by the agency would not be against equity and good conscience despite
the absence of fault on the part of the employee. John Wessels, B-265874, May 22,
1996.
As noted by POD, the issue in this case is whether Mr. Naylor can be said to be
at fault in this matter as that term is used in the statute. The standard employed by
the Comptroller General and OHA is to determine whether a reasonable person
should have been aware that he was receiving a payment to which he was not
entitled. Where the reasonable person would have made inquiry, but the employee
did not, then he is not free from fault and the claim cannot be waived. John H.
Young, Jr., B-253640, November 4, 1993.
In this case, Mr. Naylor’s pay and personnel records would not have alerted
him to the fact that an error had occurred. Generally, where an employee has
documentary records, such as Forms SF-50 (Notification of Personnel Action) and
L&E (Leave and Earnings) statements, and fails to review those documents for
accuracy or otherwise fails to take corrective action, he is not without fault and
waiver will be denied. Id.; Gordon Field, M.D., B-224910, June 22, 1987.
Comptroller General decisions have held that if a reasonable person would have
inquired about the correctness of a payment, but the employee did not, then the
employee is not free from fault and the claim may not be waived. Simon B. Guedea,
B-189385, August 10, 1997, and cases cited.
Fault exists if, in light of all the facts, it is determined that an employee
exercising reasonable diligence should have known that an error existed and would
38 OHA 71

D 2008-10
have taken action to see to it that the error was corrected. In re Mary Ann Slim,
18 OHA 57, 58-59 (1999). If so, the employee had the obligation to set aside the
overpayment and hold it for repayment to the Government when the error was
corrected. Anthony Sideris, B-259124, Feb. 23, 1995.
Decisions of the Comptroller General and this Office have held that waiver of
overpayments may be granted where the agency improperly fixed the employee’s pay
rate, and it appeared that the employee was not familiar with the pay regulations,
and was not furnished with pay or personnel records which, if examined, would have
led to the discovery of the error. In this case, the personnel records provided to
Mr. Naylor incorrectly indicated that he was still non-exempt after his promotion.
We find that Mr. Naylor had no reason to believe that his FLSA status was incorrectly
coded. In re Barbara I. Martin, B-206674, March 25, 1982.
In summary, on the basis of the record before us, we find that Mr. Naylor is
without fault in this matter, and that it would be against equity and good conscience
and the best interests of the United States to deny his request for waiver of Bill for
Collection No. M0723200005 (for $10,768.01) and Bill for Collection No.
71980065479 (for $1,564.91) in the total amount of $12,332.92. Accordingly, the
waiver request submitted by Mr. Naylor is hereby granted.
Pursuant to 344 DM 9, this decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter.
